articles.title_orig: China Fears A.I. Could Give the U.S. an Edge in Nuclear Rivalry
articles.title_zh: China Fears A.I. Could Give the U.S. an Edge in Nuclear Rivalry
articles.content_orig:
Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney shakes hands with China's President Xi Jinping at the APEC summit on Nov. 19, 2026.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is placing particular focus on renewing relations with China as he aims to deepen international trade ties and diversify from U.S. reliance amid a three-month-long trade war with the U.S.
When asked what cards Canada holds in its ongoing talks with Washington, Carney, who recently announced a new partnership with the E.U. , pointed to the country's budding relationships elsewhere.
“Our cards are that everyone else in the world wants to deal with us,” he said Wednesday during a remote interview with the New York Times from Shenzhen, China, where he was among the world leaders attending the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit . "If the U.S. doesn't want to do the deal, we're busy.” His remarks came in the wake of President Donald Trump's claim that the U.S. holds “all the cards” after trade talks collapsed in August, leading to both sides enforcing heavy retaliatory tariffs .
Carney and Trump had a meeting on the sidelines of APEC, but aside from a commitment to “continue” negotiations and stay in close contact, no progress was made. However, Carney painted his meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping in a much more positive light. Ahead of the summit, Carney and Xi announced a Canada-China trade pact , which provided additional tariff relief on Canadian food and agricultural exports into China, and in return saw Canada agree to extend tariff exemptions for certain Chinese steel and aluminum products by two years.
Carney, who is promoting a “Canada Strong” platform as he aims to build economic resilience at home, touted the expansion of the trade arrangement with China as something that will deliver “greater certainty and prosperity for all Canadians.” He also praised the negotiation process with China, saying: “They’re very professional. They move forward in a very linear fashion.”
In an eight-day tour that took him from a European summit in Ireland to the Philippines, Cambodia, and finally China for the APEC gathering, Carney forged ahead with his plan to diversify Canada's economy away from its dependence on the U.S., which by far remains the country's largest trading partner .
Experts say Canada's progress in deepening its economic relationships with China could challenge Trump's insistence that Washington holds the upper hand in trade negotiations.
“Part of the Trump Administration’s [belief] is that everybody needs the U.S. more than anything else, and therefore the U.S. has maximum leverage,” says Jennifer Hillman, co-director of the Institute of International Economic Law at Georgetown University. “What this is clearly saying is that Canada can afford to be less willing to give the U.S. whatever it asks for [in negotiations], because they have other options.”
China has the world's second-largest economy , behind only the U.S., giving it the potential to become a much larger market for Canadian goods than some of the other countries Carney has sought to deepen relations with.
“China represents a very big market and the potential of a really big trading partner,” says Lori Turnbull, a professor in the Faculty of Management at Dalhousie University, noting it could be a leverage point in U.S. negotiations. “Doing a deal with a country like China is something that [the U.S.] will care about because of the size of China's economy and its competitive relationship with the U.S.”
Carney's latest push to strengthen trade ties with Beijing forms part of a months-long effort to renew Canada-China relations. In January, he met with Xi to forge what he called a “ new strategic partnership ,” agreeing to allow in up to 49,000 Chinese electric vehicles at a tariff of 6.1%, rather than the previous 100% levy. China agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural products, including canola seeds, a major Canadian export.
The move drew criticism from Trump, who said that “China will eat Canada alive, completely devour it, including the destruction of their businesses, social fabric, and general way of life.”
While Canada's closer relationship with China could strengthen its hand in negotiations, experts also warn that it could backfire.
Turnbull points to the latest agreement to extend tariff exemptions on Chinese steel and aluminum as a potential source of tension with Washington. “Things like reducing tariffs on select steel and aluminum products coming from China is something that might make the U.S. and not just Donald Trump, but also [U.S. Trade Representative] Jamieson Greer angry,” she suggests.
Steel, aluminum, and auto tariffs were among the major points of contention when U.S.-Canada trade negotiations broke down in August, with both sides accusing each other of walking back commitments.
Carney, however, has played down concerns that Canada's growing trade relationship with China is a major issue for Trump.
“In my conversation with the President, he’s tried to understand where we are with China, where we’re going with China,” said Carney during a news conference in Shenzhen. “I shouldn’t speak for him, but in his hierarchy of issues, it’s not the top issue at all.”
Meanwhile, some Canadian officials have voiced concerns on expanding trade with China.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford warned Carney on Monday against opening the door for more Chinese-made EV vehicles in Canada, arguing the “government’s focus needs to be on protecting Canadian auto workers, not undermining them by importing even more state-subsidized cheap Chinese cars.”
Michael Chong, a lawmaker from Canada’s Conservative Party, during a press conference on Wednesday supported maintaining a dialogue with Beijing, but described Carney’s budding strategic partnership with China as a “risky gambit,” citing potential “national security” concerns.
In 2025, Ottawa identified China as one of the main perpetrators of foreign interference and espionage against Canada alongside other countries such as Russia and Iran. The Canadian government’s own analysis of Canada-China relations also points out that there are "associated risks” in broader trade cooperation in key areas, such as “prevalent and persistent intellectual property theft, and the risk of diversion of sensitive goods and technologies intended for civilian use for military purposes and applications.”
Carney said ahead of his Asia trip that he would raise concerns about foreign interference in his meeting with Xi. "The advantage of these meetings is you can raise issues directly and frankly,” he told reporters in Montreal on Nov. 10. Carney added that he would stress the importance Canada places on "the non-interference in our affairs by China and other countries.”
In a press briefing during the APEC summit, Carney emphasized that Canada's trade with China is largely focused on commodities, rather than sensitive technologies such as advanced semiconductors.
“We are exporting canola, we are exporting pork. We are exporting halibut,” Carney said , also citing liquefied natural gas and oil. “These are important industries. These are not cutting-edge semi-conductors.”
Experts point out that Canada could pursue deeper cooperation with other international partners in sectors where a closer relationship with China would be more difficult, including defense and advanced technology.
“[Canada] is not going to partner with China on defense, security, AI, and digital technology, things like that would be very difficult. [Carney] would have an impossible time trying to convince Canadians that's what we should be doing,” says Turnbull. “For those things, [Canada] would be putting [its] arms around the European Union.”
In September, the European Union unveiled its vision for Canada to become an “associate member” of the bloc. During an E.U.-Canada summit in Montreal in October, the two sides underscored their commitment to this plan, paving the way for deeper cooperation in areas including A

articles.title_orig: Boy, 7, pulled alive from rubble hours after Russian strike on Ukraine, rescuers say
articles.title_zh: Boy, 7, pulled alive from rubble hours after Russian strike on Ukraine, rescuers say
articles.content_orig:
'Danger seems greater all the time': Ukrainians search for missing after Russian strikes hit Kyiv
A seven-year-old boy has been rescued from the rubble of a residential building in Dymer after 14 hours, in overnight Russian strikes on Dymer, in the Kyiv region, that killed ten people, Ukrainian officials have said.
The attack occurred in the early hours of Sunday. A 79-year-old woman was also rescued alive from the collapsed building, Kyiv's regional head Tymur Tkachenko said.
A strike on a private home in Bila Tserkva killed one more person and set the building ablaze, he added.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky also said three people were killed and 13 wounded in a separate strike on Vyshneve, also in the Kyiv region, that hit a grocery store on Sunday.
Ukrainian authorities said the boy in Dymer is in stable condition and was taken to hospital, and have thanked everyone involved in saving his life.
Zelensky and Ukraine's national police also confirmed the rescue of the boy.
Response teams including police, explosive technicians, dog handlers and medics are continuing with rescue efforts.
In a telegram post, Tkachenko said the 79-year-old woman rescued from the rubble was receiving treatment in hospital.
Earlier he said six people were injured in the attack, while others were still missing.
The attack on the residential building occurred in the early hours of the morning while people were asleep
Zelensky said more than 130 people are involved in emergency operations at the scene, and that they will continue until they have "complete information about every single person".
Sending his condolences to the families and loved ones of those killed, he said the strike struck the residential building, "practically blowing a section of it to smithereens".
Zelensky added that "rescue efforts are complicated by constant new air raid alerts and renewed threats".
The strike hit the building at 05:00 local time, when families were still asleep, Ukraine's minister of internal affairs Ivan Vyhivskyi said.
More than 70 strikes have been launched across 10 Ukrainian regions as of Sunday evening, Vyhivskyi added.
Emergency workers continue to search for those missing after Russian drone and missile attacks in Dymer.
In his video address posted online, Zelensky also said three people were killed and 13 injured in a strike on an "ordinary grocery store" in Vyshneve.
Mayor Illya Dikov wrote on social media that three children were among the injured.
Russia also struck a power substation in the Dnipropetrovsk region, Ukraine's Prime Minister Sergiy Koretsky said in a post on X. , external

articles.title_orig: US Stock Futures Rally After AI Rout, Havens Fall: Markets Wrap
articles.title_zh: US Stock Futures Rally After AI Rout, Havens Fall: Markets Wrap
articles.content_orig:
U.S. equity futures bounced on Sunday, as a shortened week on Wall Street got underway after all three major averages ended Friday in correction territory .
Futures tied to the Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 673 points, or 1.4%. S&P 500 futures added 2.03%, and Nasdaq-100 futures rose 2.76%.
In Asia, South Korea's Kospi fell 3.16%, with heavyweights Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix down about 3.6% and 3.2%, respectively. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 was marginally down. Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index slipped 1.27% on its open, and mainland China's CSI 300 fell 0.58%. Japan's markets were closed for a public holiday.
Last week, major indexes tumbled as worries about the artificial intelligence trade continued to spook investors, despite Anthropic's record debut on Thursday.
By the end of the rout last week — which was the worst weekly decline for the Nasdaq Composite and Dow in more than six years, and the largest for the S&P 500 since April 2025 — all three of the major averages were in correction territory, and the Nasdaq turned negative for the year.
The Nasdaq-100 index ended Friday in bear market territory on an intraday basis, but was just shy of that mark based on the decline from its closing high on Oct. 6.
Investors this week will get a breather, no matter what price action looks like. Markets are closed on Thursday for the Thanksgiving holiday, and Friday's session will be shortened with the closing bell set to ring at 1:00 p.m.
All eyes are set to be on the shaky tech trade, as investors examine if last week's sell-off represented the market finding a durable bottom, or if equities have more room to fall.
Drew Pettit, chief investment strategist at Roundhill, said in an appearance on CNBC's " Closing Bell: Overtime " on Friday that the indiscriminate selling at the end of the week — which extended beyond just tech — is a sign the sell-off may be concluding. But, he said the burden of proof is on the bulls to undermine the bearish sentiment dominating the market.
"Fundamentally, I think the floor is a lot higher," he said about how low equities could go. "Technically… you need a string of catalysts for the bulls to prove the long-term earnings story isn't broken."
Tata Steel , one of the world's leading steel producers, on Monday said it will buy a 26.4% stake in India's largest structural steel pipe and tube maker, APL Apollo , for 155.1 billion rupees ($1.67 billion).
Shares of Tata Steel were nearly 5% lower on Monday, while APL Apollo shares tanked over 16% in early trade.
The acquisition will boost Tata Steel's downstream integration to around 53% from 35%, Tata Steel said in a stock exchange filing. That will lead to more value addition, improved product mix, and greater exposure to higher-margin downstream segments, it said.
Asian markets kickstarted the week on a lower note, extending the sell-off from the previous week.
South Korea's Kospi fell 2.34% in early trading, while the small-cap Kosdaq was flat, with heavyweights Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix down about 3% and 2%, respectively.
Australia's S&P/ASX 200 was 0.11% down.
Asia markets were set to open lower Monday, after a sharp sell-off last week as investors soured on AI plays.
Australia's S&P/ASX 200 started the day down 0.49%, on pace for its eighth straight session of losses.
Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index futures indicated a lower open for the market, standing at 22,238 compared to the index's last close of 22,410.8. The HSI has posted losses for four straight sessions.
Japan's markets are closed for a public holiday.
Analyst Dan Ives said in a Sunday note to clients the panic in the market related to the artificial intelligence trades rivals other major sell-offs this decade.
"We are going through a tech sell-off that we would equate fear and anxiety wise with the March 2020 Covid days and April 2025 Liberation moments," he said, referring with the latter example to the market's reaction when President Donald Trump first introduced his global tariff scheme .
The Yorkville Ives & Co. partner and senior managing director warned there could be more room for stocks to fall, but he added the fundamentals of the AI trade are strong and that any downward movements will likely be temporary.
"This will be bumpy road over the coming months. That said, the technology age of AI is coming one way or another … and this is not going to slow down the 160 GW of backlog/demand power through 2029."
Despite the shortened trading week, there are still key companies that are set to deliver earnings over the period.
Two key hardware companies — Hewlett Packard Enterprise and Dell Technologies — will deliver their quarterly results on Monday and Tuesday, respectively, after the bell. Both have tumbled sharply this month, with HPE down 25% and Dell off 34%, amid the sell-off among companies with exposure to the artificial intelligence buildout.
Meanwhile, electronics retailer Best Buy is set to deliver results before the bell on Tuesday, while software company Workday will share its financials after hours on the same day.
U.S. equity futures jumped to begin trading Sunday evening, seeking to rebound from Friday's sell-off.
Futures tied to the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 412 points, or 0.8%. S&P 500 futures advanced 1.1%, while Nasdaq-100 futures rose 1.9%.

articles.title_orig: Yemen's Houthis claim attacks on Saudi oil refinery as Trump warns of new strikes next year
articles.title_zh: Yemen's Houthis claim attacks on Saudi oil refinery as Trump warns of new strikes next year
articles.content_orig:
Yemen's Houthis, backed by Iran, said Sunday that they had targeted Rabigh oil refinery in Saudi Arabia, in the latest sign of worsening hostilities in the region, as Iranian forces seek to pressure the U.S. into accepting its terms.
The Houthis said they has directly hit the infrastructure, though the extent of the damage remains unclear, Reuters reported.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said earlier in the day that it had "intercepted and destroyed" a drone launched by the Houthis toward Saudi Arabia's western region, which included some of the country's critical energy refining and export infrastructure.
Rabigh, about 165 kilometers north of Jeddah on the kingdom's western Red Sea coast, hosts Petro Rabigh, a major oil refining and petrochemical complex, developed by Saudi Aramco and Japan's Sumitomo Chemical.
Saudi Arabia's Ministry of Interior did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment.
Gulf countries reported multiple attacks by Iran-linked forces over the weekend, even as the country's foreign minister said his government remains open to a negotiated end to the war. Bahrain authorities said an Iranian attack on a civilian industrial facility injured two people on Saturday.
The string of attacks mark the latest sign of escalation in the regional hostilities since the war between the U.S.-Israel and Iran began in late February, as negotiators have so far failed to agree on terms to end the monthslong war.
The conflict has drawn in countries in the Gulf region, disrupting energy flows through the Strait of Hormuz, which used to carry a fifth of the world's crude shipments prior to the war, pushing up global prices for oil and commodities.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations reported another incident involving a tanker and military forces in the Gulf of Oman on Sunday, after two tankers were struck by unknown projectiles the day before. The maritime agency gave no further details about the incident, urging vessels to stay vigilant about the operational environment.
Tehran has indicated its intention to end the war with the U.S. through diplomacy, but President Donald Trump has dismissed Iranian proposals. Both sides have been in indirect communication via Qatar.
In an interview to Fox News on Saturday, Trump warned that he was inclined to order military strikes against Tehran next year, if the two countries failed to finalize an agreement. The president blamed the Iranian officials for stalling while escalating hostilities after the U.S. elections.
"They're more aggressive now than before the election," Trump said, describing Iranian officials as "professional tap dancers." "They talk all the time, all they do is talk," he added.
The president has previously said that Tehran wants a deal to end hostilities but not one that is "acceptable" to him. He has oscillated between favoring an agreement that would end the fighting and insisting that the U.S. does not need to rush into any deal and is not afraid of resuming more aggressive attacks.
The Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said Saturday after a two-hour meeting with visiting Qatari mediators that, "We are in contact with mediators, including the Qataris, both in person and virtually, and are holding the necessary discussions to see whether another opportunity can be given to diplomacy," according to Reuters .
International benchmark Brent futures inched 0.22% lower to $92.35 per barrel in early Asia trading hours, while WTI crude was down 0.19% at $83.25 a barrel.

articles.title_orig: Medical student, 24, suddenly dies of ‘food poisoning’ during graduation trip to Turkey — but family skeptical
articles.title_zh: Medical student, 24, suddenly dies of ‘food poisoning’ during graduation trip to Turkey — but family skeptical
articles.content_orig:
A young and healthy Canadian medical student died suddenly during a celebratory trip to Turkey last year — reportedly due to food poisoning, but her family is now speaking out, saying the evidence doesn’t add up.
Bérengère Deveaux-Cattino, a 24-year-old from Montreal, died while celebrating her graduation from medical school with her friends in Istanbul on June 17, 2025.
Deveaux-Cattino and her pals ventured through tourist sites before landing in the bustling city two days before their trip ended, CBC reported.
“She’d never been to Turkey,” her sister, Éléonore Deveaux-Cattino, told the outlet. “She thought it was a super beautiful, vibrant country.”
After checking into a hotel, Deveaux-Cattino had a chicken casserole, Turkish tea, and baklava — a meal that caused the group to wake up violently ill, the outlet reported.
A woman who traveled with Deveaux-Cattino, who used the name Laurie to protect her identity, said the friends all started throwing up within minutes of waking up.
“Then I started feeling unwell,” Laurie said, “and suddenly we were taking turns running to the bathroom to vomit until we realized that whatever it was, it wasn’t just going to pass.”
During the bout of intense sickness, Deveaux-Cattino FaceTimed her sister Éléonore, sparking concern among her family.
“I thought: ‘This isn’t normal. Something’s off. This is going to be bad news,'” said Éléonore Deveaux-Cattino. “She says, ‘Élo, we’re in the hospital in Istanbul, and things aren’t going well. I’ve been told to contact the family.'”
Her sister and their father, Henri Cattino, scrambled to find flights to Istanbul, but heard the tragic news while waiting for a connecting flight in Paris.
“I said: ‘Please, can you tell me if my sister has died?'” said Éléonore Deveaux-Cattino. “And she said: ‘I’m very sorry, Éléonore, but your sister is dead.'”
The Deveaux-Cattinos repatriated Bérengère’s body and contacted the Quebec coroner’s office, but buried her with her cause of death still a mystery.
In November, a Turkish-German family of four, the Böceks, became violently sick and died within three days of their trip to Istanbul — after staying in a hotel just blocks away from where Bérengère fell ill.
Investigators initially believed food poisoning was the cause, but days later, authorities suspected that aluminum phosphide, a highly toxic agricultural pesticide used to kill rodents and insects, might have been responsible for their deaths.
The owners of the pest control company involved in the fatal poisoning were sentenced to 18 years behind bars, and the hotel owners and employees were sentenced to roughly 12 to 13 years.
Aluminum phosphide, also known as “the bomb,” is used in pellet form and releases dangerous phosphine gas when exposed to air — killing every living thing in a room within 72 hours.
Though the pesticide is illegal in urban areas, Istanbul has a bedbug problem, and desperate homeowners sometimes resort to “gassing” the gnarly critters.
Fumigation in the hotel room next to the Böcek family was determined to be the cause of their death, the outlet reported.
“We tell them their neighbors could die from it, and that they could, too. But they say: ‘We have no choice, it’s the only thing that works,'” exterminator Birkan Cihan said.
The same pesticide also killed Audrey and Noémi Bélanger, two sisters from Quebec, in Thailand in 2012.
The Deveaux-Cattinos eventually received the autopsy report concluding that Bérengère Deveaux-Cattino died of food poisoning — but evidence from the Quebec coroner’s report poked holes in the ruling.
“The coroner here ran some tests, and she couldn’t confirm that food poisoning was the cause of death because, usually, there are signs of intestinal irritation,” Éléonore Deveaux-Cattino said.
“There were none in my sister’s case.”
The outlet, alongside Ayse Adanali, a freelance Turkish journalist, found that there were 30 cases of phosphine poisoning and a dozen related deaths in Turkey since 2023.
“This is not food poisoning,” Sebnem Korur Fincancıs, a leading forensic pathologist in Turkey, told the outlet after reading Bérengère Deveaux-Cattino’s Turkish autopsy report.
“I don’t think that this is food poisoning because there is no story of diarrhea, only throwing up,” Fincancıs said. “Rather, it is the pesticide poisoning.”
The pathologist also noticed metabolic acidosis in the autopsy report, a hallmark of phosphine gas poisoning, which involves increased acidity in the body.
“There is the metabolic acidosis, which also indicates the pesticide intoxication,” she said. “It is one of the main findings of these kinds of cases.”
“With all these misdiagnoses, we have to consider the situation.”
The outlet also found evidence of a possible bedbug infestation at the Seven Days Hotel where Bérengère Deveaux-Cattino stayed, including in the room next door to hers.
Hotel manager Bahattin Demir told the outlet that an exterminator sprayed the rooms monthly but said he didn’t believe the pesticide was used.
The hotel’s pest-control contractor, Wolves, also denied using the aluminum phosphide, but in an undercover call arranged by CBC, an employee described a bedbug treatment that would require sealing a room for 72 hours.
“For 72 hours, nobody goes in, the doors are locked and nothing living enters,” the employee said.
Without a confirmation of her sister’s cause of death, Éléonore Deveaux-Cattino said she wants to give her a voice.
“My sister is younger than me. I’d never imagined a life without her. We used to be two against the world … now I’m all alone,” she said.
“But I’m stubborn. And since she can no longer speak, I’ll speak for her. I’ll never let her go.”

articles.title_orig: Explosion on Russian ship at Libya port caused by suspected drone attack, officials say
articles.title_zh: Explosion on Russian ship at Libya port caused by suspected drone attack, officials say
articles.content_orig:
An explosion on a Russian ship docked at Benghazi naval base was caused by a suspected drone attack, Libya's eastern government has said.
The explosion happened at dawn on Sunday, while the ship had stopped for fuel and supplies on its way back to Russia, Libya state media reported, citing the eastern government.
The statement said there were no casualties. Moscow has yet to comment.
Later on Sunday, the health ministry said it had received injured people from another vessel, a commercial ship, that was also targeted off the coast of Benghazi, state media reported. Their injuries were minor and their condition stable, the ministry said.
The UN mission in Libya expressed "serious concern" over the attacks, calling for "an immediate, independent and transparent investigation".
"Libya cannot afford, and must not become a battleground for foreign conflicts," the UNSMIL wrote on X.
Videos posted on social media and geolocated by BBC Verify show the ship that was struck in the morning engulfed in flames and smoke. Satellite imagery from Planet Labs PBC also shows a boat on fire at 05:47 GMT at the Benghazi port.
US-based intelligence firm Vantor collected high-resolution images that it said showed Project 20380 Steregushchiy-class corvette (Merkury) - a Russian navy ship - moored in the port on Saturday, and on Sunday showed most of the same ship capsized and sunk with only the forward bow still visible.
The eastern-based Government of National Stability (GNS) said the Russian ship - which it did not name or identify - was using the Benghazi port within the framework of an existing maritime agreement.
Sunday's incident is under investigation, and authorities are coordinating with their Russian counterparts to determine the source of the suspected attack and who is responsible for it, GNS added.
GNS condemned the attack on a ship inside a Libyan port, and called it a violation of maritime safety and an attack on their sovereignty. It said Libya was not party to the Russia-Ukraine war, or any other conflict beyond its borders.
Separately, Libya's internationally recognised government in Tripoli - the Government of National Unity (GNU) - warned against hosting foreign forces and allowing them to use facilities in a statement published by state media.
GNU said such activity raises "serious fears" about "risks that may result from involving ports and civilian facilities in activities related to external conflicts, and the resulting threat to the lives of citizens and the safety of national facilities and assets".
Libya fractured into violence and instability after its leader Muammar Gaddafi was overthrown in 2011, leading to the opposing governments.
Benghazi is more than 2,000 km (1,243 miles) away from the Russian capital Moscow.
Although it has not been officially confirmed who was behind the attack, there is little doubt, according to Jalel Harchaoui, Libya specialist at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI).
"Ukraine is the only actor brazen enough to pull something like that off," he told the BBC. "If I were to bet my own money, I would bet that it was the Ukrainians."
If confirmed, it would not be the first time Ukrainian forces had carried out an operation of this sort. In March, Russia accused Ukraine of targeting the Russian tanker Arctic Metagaz in the Mediterranean between Libya and Malta with "uncrewed sea drones" launched from the Libyan coast.
As well as having an economic impact on Russia, hampering the ability of their so-called shadow fleet of tankers to export oil and gas, attacks like this are seen as humiliating to the Kremlin, according to Harchaoui.
But it is not only Moscow that will want to react to this latest incident. The ship was in the region as part of a deal with the government of eastern Libya - allied with Khalifa Haftar, commander of the Libyan National Army.
Harchaoui said Haftar will take the attack as a personal slight. "You're going to have a response by the Haftar family. They will ask questions about who is hosting the Ukrainians."
Additional reporting by Benedict Garman and Shayan Sardarizadeh

articles.title_orig: It will soon be too late to regulate use of autonomous weapons, warns Red Cross
articles.title_zh: It will soon be too late to regulate use of autonomous weapons, warns Red Cross
articles.content_orig:
Warning about putting ‘genie back in the bottle’ comes as UN conference fails to agree on regulation instrument
The International Committee of the Red Cross and rights groups have warned that it will soon be too late to put the “genie back in the bottle” as the development of autonomous weapons appears to outpace efforts to regulate them.
The stark warning came as more than 120 member states of the UN Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons concluded a week-long conference in Geneva.
Despite mounting pressure, an agreement to discuss an instrument to regulate autonomous weapons over the next two years fell short of the urgent action rights groups said was needed to address the looming threat.
“We’re starting to see artificial intelligence … being fielded in the battlefield and perhaps also already in weapon systems. If we leave this unregulated, it will be much more difficult to put the genie back in the bottle,” said Dr Cordula Droege, the director of international law, movement and partnerships at the ICRC.
Autonomous weapons are military systems that act without human supervision, often through the use of artificial intelligence or other forms of robotics.
As artificial intelligence has grown exponentially in recent years, militaries and manufacturers have created increasingly advanced weapons systems for both offensive and defensive purposes.
These systems include the use of AI in generating target banks , as was done by the Israeli military in Gaza, as well as semi-autonomous drones in the Ukraine-Russia war, which have “last-mile capability”, where AI takes over in the drone’s final approach to its target.
The president of the ICRC, Mirjana Spoljaric Egger, and the UN secretary general, António Guterres, have called for a legally binding instrument with clear prohibitions and restrictions on use of weapons. In particular, the ICRC has called for a ban on the use of autonomous weapons against personnel, as well as ensuring that weapons systems behave predictably and placing limits on weapons including restricting their use to military objectives.
Experts have said that given the rapid development of autonomous weapons and AI, the failure to create adequate regulations could have dangerous repercussions.
“It’s not about banning all autonomous weapon systems, but to set limits in an international treaty of red lines that should never be crossed,” said Droege. “We’re very close to crossing those red lines, particularly targeting human beings through machines should be a moral red line.”
Other rights groups warned that any delay towards regulation of these weapons risked allowing private industry and militaries to set the norms of how autonomous weapons are used.
Already, autonomous weapons have led to civilian harm. Three civilians were killed by a Russian drone guided by an AI system in July in Zaporizhzhia in south-eastern Ukraine. The drone tried to hit a petrol station, probably its intended target, but instead crashed into a wall, killing three people in a fountain of shrapnel.
In Gaza, Israel has used AI-assisted targeting methods to fill its target banks much faster than humanly possible since the start of the war. As a result, rights groups have said that civilians and people with tenuous links to militant groups were erroneously killed.
In Iran, a US strike that hit an elementary school, killing 156 civilians including 120 schoolchildren, reportedly was a result of faulty intelligence gathered by AI systems.
Anna Hehir, the head of military AI governance at the Future of Life Institute, said further delay to a strong treaty could see “more cases of mass civilian harm that we’ve seen over the past 18 months to two years”, warning that some of these mass casualty events could dwarf what has already occurred. She said manufacturers and militaries were trying to develop “swarm” capabilities, where hundreds or thousands of autonomous drones act at the same time.
“This has the potential for high damage, just because of the sheer mass of systems that would be autonomous. All it takes is for one of them to face algorithmic error and then the entire swarm is utilised and led down a path based on that error … particularly if they’re programmed to target humans.”
There is also a risk of proliferation, as non-state groups increasingly use AI to program their weapons systems, as was the case when the Houthi movement in Yemen used Claude to “vibe code” ballistic missiles.
Armed Islamist groups in Africa’s Sahel region have reportedly used AI tools to improve drone ballistics and for operational planning.
“This is the only thing that is important this week. It’s not really the substance of laws. What’s on the agenda here, after 13 years, is the political will finally present to start to get serious about regulation of autonomous weapons systems,” said a senior diplomat with knowledge of the UN discussions.

articles.title_orig: U.S. Tracked Alice Huang’s Contacts With China Spy Agency During Nvidia Affair
articles.title_zh: U.S. Tracked Alice Huang’s Contacts With China Spy Agency During Nvidia Affair
articles.content_orig:
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said the U.S. is investigating Alice Huang and her former company, Megaspeed, as a report identified one of her associates as a key decision-maker at the Singapore-based company.
Alice Huang, with whom ousted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang reportedly had a romantic relationship, was a key figure in Megaspeed International, a cloud computing firm that operates data centers across Southeast Asia linked to the fallout surrounding the leadership shake-up.
"There is an investigation ongoing into her firm and into her," Clayton told ABC on Sunday, adding that, "Nvidia chips, they are the jewel. They are the absolute top that everybody wants, that's why we're focusing on this."
Alice Huang's associate, Chinese national Li Ming, who is now out on bail in Singapore, was "deeply involved" in Megaspeed's activities and took part in major decisions, The Wall Street Journal reported earlier on Saturday, citing people familiar with the matter.
The Singapore charges against Li concern alleged false representations to Super Micro Computer, a U.S.-based firm with known links to chipmaker Nvidia, though Megaspeed is not named in those charges.
Last week , the Commerce and Justice departments said that the investigation into Megaspeed began in 2024 over potential export-control violations. Their joint statement said Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security and Singapore law enforcement interviewed Huang during an on-site check in June 2025.
The Justice Department later took the lead in the criminal investigation.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CBS on Sunday that the administration was seeking answers from Nvidia about its chip sales to China, including who oversaw compliance and which levels of the company knew about the activity.
Separately, The New York Times reported Sunday that Alice Huang was in contact with an officer of a top Chinese intelligence agency from spring 2025 through fall 2026, citing people briefed on U.S. intelligence reports.
Bloomberg reported last week that the Justice Department is investigating whether entities linked to Alice Huang helped smuggle Super Micro products to China.
Li faces five charges in Singapore, including two counts of fraud by false representation, along with allegations involving the operation of a company he controlled, unauthorized bank-account access and another company director's duties.
Prosecutors allege he falsely told Super Micro that the company would hold and lease the servers it purchased.
The Journal reported that Li is out on bail and that his case is ongoing. He was offered bail of S$1 million in March 2025. The Singapore charges do not name Megaspeed.
Earlier this month, Singapore's Ministry of Home Affairs said that police had found insufficient evidence to establish that Alice Huang committed offenses related to the possible inaccurate declarations under investigation.
The ministry said she was issued a stern warning for providing information that police assessed as knowingly inaccurate and for downplaying her role at Megaspeed. It also said Singapore had not investigated her for espionage.
Megaspeed has said it is a "legitimate and lawful business" and that Huang left the company in August 2025.
The scrutiny is set to intensify in Washington. Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and the company's general counsel, Tim Teter, have agreed to closed-door, transcribed interviews with three House committees on Dec. 1 and Dec. 2, respectively.
The committees said they want answers about Nvidia's role in allowing Chinese actors to access advanced chips and the involvement of a potential Chinese intelligence asset.
Speaking to CNBC's Squawk Box on Sunday U.S. time, Ryan Fedasiuk, a former advisor for U.S.-China Bilateral Affairs at the State Department, said that there was "still a lot we don't know" about the case.
He said lawmakers would likely focus on Nvidia's customer relationships and "who knew what at the company when."
Fedasiuk added that there was "a very good chance" investigators would find that people at Nvidia knew their products could be used for restricted purposes. He characterized the existing evidence as containing "multiple" smoking guns.

articles.title_orig: COP31 Talks Collapse in Turkey in a Clash Over Fossil Fuels
articles.title_zh: COP31 Talks Collapse in Turkey in a Clash Over Fossil Fuels
articles.content_orig:
The COP31 climate conference in Antalya, Turkey, collapsed Sunday as countries failed to agree to an overarching deal after more than two weeks of contentious negotiations. The breaking point was over the very cause of climate change itself: fossil fuels.
The annual UN climate talks, which stretched deep into overtime over the weekend, hold the dubious honor of being the longest COP in history and the first major breakdown since COP15 in Copenhagen in 2009.
Experts criticized the conference as a stunning failure of leadership at a time when the climate crisis is accelerating with increasingly deadly consequences. “This has been the worst ever COP and its collapse needs to be a wake up call for the world,” said Mohamed Adow, director of the energy think tank Power Shift Africa.
How two words could derail the world’s biggest climate conference
At the final meeting intended to approve the so-called Antalya Pact on Sunday, it became clear there would not be the necessary consensus between the more than 190 countries at the talks to adopt the deal. These did not include the US, which, under President Donald Trump, has pulled out of international climate action.
Deep divisions proved impossible to bridge over key issues — most importantly, including language that the world would need to move away from fossil fuels, a phrase that did not end up in the agreement, and increasing financial support for countries already grappling with climate catastrophes. Petrostates, including Saudi Arabia, have long opposed the inclusion of any reference to fossil fuels.
The European Union, Panama, the Marshall Islands and Norway were among those that rejected it. Darragh O’Brien, Ireland’s climate minister who is helping lead negotiations for the EU, said the bloc would not endorse a deal “that does not even mention fossil fuels.”
“This COP, I believe, was hijacked by some oil states,” he later told Reuters news agency.
COP31 president Murat Kurum acknowledged support was not there to gavel through the pact. “We have done our utmost,” he said, but “it is clear that there are parties in this hall who oppose this text. We recognize that there is no consensus on this document.”
This invisible, super-polluting gas is a climate villain the world is failing to tackle
China, which is the world’s biggest climate polluter but also a clean energy superpower , called the lack of consensus a “deep disappointment.” Chinese delegation head Li Gao said the outcome shouldn’t “lead to a loss of confidence” in countries’ ability to work together to address climate change, Chinese state media Xinhua reported.
The talks come at a critical time for the planet. While attention is diverted by geopolitical turbulence — including the Iran war, which has caused the world’s largest energy supply shock — the climate crisis is accelerating.
A sobering recent UN report confirmed the world will overshoot its target of limiting global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels. On current policies temperatures are expected to rise to a potentially catastrophic 2.8 degrees. The planet is currently at around 1.4 degrees of warming and the impacts have been starkly clear, from catastrophic flooding in Nepal to deadly heat in Europe.
Yet, COP31 laid bare the enormous gap between those seeking ambitious action, often the most climate-vulnerable countries, and the oil-rich nations pushing back.
In common with previous COPs, the biggest sticking point came down to two words: fossil fuels.
At COP28 in Dubai in 2023, countries agreed to an unprecedented call to “transition away from fossil fuels.” Since then, this has neither been repeated nor built upon as oil-producing nations balk at any reference to the driving force of the climate crisis.
200,000 walruses are forced ashore in Alaska as sea ice melts. Now there’s a plan to protect them
The first draft of the COP31 “cover decision” — which sets out the overarching agreement from the conference — was published Monday and called for “the immediate transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems.”
But all mentions of fossil fuels were stripped out of every subsequent draft, despite a push by more than 100 countries to keep them in. “You cannot solve a fossil fuel crisis by pretending we don’t need to phase out fossil fuels,” said Harjeet Singh, COP negotiations veteran and founding director of Satat Sampada Climate Foundation.
Britain’s lead climate negotiator Kate Hughes said the proposed agreement “moves us backwards,” describing it as “a lowest common denominator, where it should have been instead presenting bold, collective ambition on climate action.”
Meanwhile, Amnesty International’s Climate Justice policy adviser, Ann Harrison, said countries were “right to reject” what she called a “polluters’ charter designed to protect corporate profits.”
Countries and climate groups were also concerned by the agreement’s reference to increasing carbon capture technologies, which would allow for a continuation of fossil fuel production provided its carbon pollution is captured before it reaches the atmosphere.
While many scientists say the amount of carbon pollution means this technology will be needed to some extent, it remains expensive, unproven at scale and criticized as a dangerous distraction from climate policies that tackle the root cause of the crisis.
“Relying on carbon capture without phasing down fossil fuels is like trying to quit smoking without putting down the cigarettes,” said Matt Webb, associate director for global clean power diplomacy at E3G, a climate think tank.
Another huge issue of contention was finance. Poorer, climate-vulnerable countries have long called for more money to help them adapt to climate disasters they disproportionately face and yet did little to cause.
Many developing countries expressed deep disappointment that the draft agreement called for effort to at least triple adaptation finance by 2035 but included no baseline and no specific numbers.
“Rich countries refused to put money on the table to help communities prepare for and recover from climate disasters, and handed polluters a free pass instead,” Singh said. “No deal is better than a deal that locks in failure.”
COP31 president of negotiations, Chris Bowen, said the result was very disappointing but there were “a lot of good things” to come out of the talks, including more than 90 countries signing a pledge to ramp up the electrification of their economies.
“What happens now is that… will continue in our renewable transition and reconvene in Ethiopia next year and see if we can’t make forward progress,” he said.
Still, many experts expressed bitter disappointment at the world’s failure to meet the urgency of the climate crisis.
“Recognition of the dangers of overshoot should have shaken leaders into action, instead COP31 saw a shameful lack of urgency and leadership,” said Mary Robinson, the former president of Ireland and a COP veteran.

articles.title_orig: Jim Beam won't resume distilling at flagship Kentucky distillery in 2027
articles.title_zh: Jim Beam won't resume distilling at flagship Kentucky distillery in 2027
articles.content_orig:
Fox News chief congressional correspondent Chad Pergram reports on Jim Beam’s decision to temporarily pause operations at its Kentucky distillery on America Reports.
Jim Beam will indefinitely pause production at its historic flagship distillery in Clermont, Kentucky, amid declining whiskey sales and record inventories.
The iconic American whiskey brand, owned by Japanese multinational brewing and distilling company Suntory Global Spirits , announced last December that it would pause production at its Clermont, Kentucky facility for one year, with plans to resume operations in 2027, Food Dive reported.
However, in a new development, it is now uncertain when the Clermont distillery will begin operations again, the company told The Courier Journal.
NEW 123.4-PROOF WHISKEY PROMPTS EXPERT WARNING THAT STRONGER ISN'T ALWAYS BETTER
Suntory told the outlet that it manages its Kentucky production in accordance with demand, inventory and long-term needs.
In December 2025, Jim Beam announced a one-year closure of its flagship distillery in Clermont, Kentucky, but announced last week that the facility will remain closed indefinitely as the company assesses production needs. (Noam Galai/Getty Images for NYCWFF and Bryan Woolston/Getty Images)
The company noted that it plans to reassess production needs in the future.
In the meantime, Jim Beam has moved production to its nearby Booker Noe Distillery in Boston, Kentucky, which, with an output of 45 million original proof gallons annually, is the brand’s largest distillery, according to Food Dive.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER
The brand's Fred B. Noe distillery, located on the Clermont facility's campus, will continue its operations producing whiskey labels including Knob Creek, Little Book and Booker's, Inc. reported.
Fox News Digital reached out to Jim Beam and the brand’s parent company, Suntory Holdings, for comment.
Whiskey inventories are at record highs in the U.S. and Kentucky in particular as consumer demand for the spirit continues to decrease. (Bryan Woolston/Getty Images)
Jim Beam’s move comes amid an ongoing decrease in consumer demand for whiskey , with large quantities of the spirit sitting untouched.
Whiskey inventory in the U.S. is three times higher than estimated annual demand, global beverage alcohol data and insight firm IWSR reported in October.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"The unifying theme across Scotch, US, Japanese and Irish whiskey is polarisation by price tier: we are seeing growth narrowing to specific bands within each whisky sub-category, rather than spreading across the price ladder," said Marten Lodewijks, IWSR managing director and president.
Jim Beam's parent company said that it remains unclear when operations will resume at the historic James B. Beam Distilling Co. distillery in Clermont, Kentucky. (Joe Hendrickson/Getty Images)
"And in most cases, that growth is concentrating at the premium end, while the mainstream and value tiers absorb the pain," he added.

Members of the Kentucky Distillers Association held an inventory of 16.1 million barrels of whiskey as of October 2025, according to the organization’s website.

Total beverage alcohol sales declined for the third consecutive year in 2025, according to IWSR.

articles.title_orig: S&P 500 futures rebound sharply to rise 2%, kick-starting shortened week after tech rout: Live updates
articles.title_zh: S&P 500 futures rebound sharply to rise 2%, kick-starting shortened week after tech rout: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
U.S. equity futures bounced on Sunday, as a shortened week on Wall Street got underway after all three major averages ended Friday in correction territory .
Futures tied to the Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 673 points, or 1.4%. S&P 500 futures added 2.03%, and Nasdaq-100 futures rose 2.76%.
In Asia, South Korea's Kospi fell 3.16%, with heavyweights Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix down about 3.6% and 3.2%, respectively. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 was marginally down. Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index slipped 1.27% on its open, and mainland China's CSI 300 fell 0.58%. Japan's markets were closed for a public holiday.
Last week, major indexes tumbled as worries about the artificial intelligence trade continued to spook investors, despite Anthropic's record debut on Thursday.
By the end of the rout last week — which was the worst weekly decline for the Nasdaq Composite and Dow in more than six years, and the largest for the S&P 500 since April 2025 — all three of the major averages were in correction territory, and the Nasdaq turned negative for the year.
The Nasdaq-100 index ended Friday in bear market territory on an intraday basis, but was just shy of that mark based on the decline from its closing high on Oct. 6.
Investors this week will get a breather, no matter what price action looks like. Markets are closed on Thursday for the Thanksgiving holiday, and Friday's session will be shortened with the closing bell set to ring at 1:00 p.m.
All eyes are set to be on the shaky tech trade, as investors examine if last week's sell-off represented the market finding a durable bottom, or if equities have more room to fall.
Drew Pettit, chief investment strategist at Roundhill, said in an appearance on CNBC's " Closing Bell: Overtime " on Friday that the indiscriminate selling at the end of the week — which extended beyond just tech — is a sign the sell-off may be concluding. But, he said the burden of proof is on the bulls to undermine the bearish sentiment dominating the market.
"Fundamentally, I think the floor is a lot higher," he said about how low equities could go. "Technically… you need a string of catalysts for the bulls to prove the long-term earnings story isn't broken."
Asian markets kickstarted the week on a lower note, extending the sell-off from the previous week.
South Korea's Kospi fell 2.34% in early trading, while the small-cap Kosdaq was flat, with heavyweights Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix down about 3% and 2%, respectively.
Australia's S&P/ASX 200 was 0.11% down.
Asia markets were set to open lower Monday, after a sharp sell-off last week as investors soured on AI plays.
Australia's S&P/ASX 200 started the day down 0.49%, on pace for its eighth straight session of losses.
Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index futures indicated a lower open for the market, standing at 22,238 compared to the index's last close of 22,410.8. The HSI has posted losses for four straight sessions.
Japan's markets are closed for a public holiday.
Analyst Dan Ives said in a Sunday note to clients the panic in the market related to the artificial intelligence trades rivals other major sell-offs this decade.
"We are going through a tech sell-off that we would equate fear and anxiety wise with the March 2020 Covid days and April 2025 Liberation moments," he said, referring with the latter example to the market's reaction when President Donald Trump first introduced his global tariff scheme .
The Yorkville Ives & Co. partner and senior managing director warned there could be more room for stocks to fall, but he added the fundamentals of the AI trade are strong and that any downward movements will likely be temporary.
"This will be bumpy road over the coming months. That said, the technology age of AI is coming one way or another … and this is not going to slow down the 160 GW of backlog/demand power through 2029."
Despite the shortened trading week, there are still key companies that are set to deliver earnings over the period.
Two key hardware companies — Hewlett Packard Enterprise and Dell Technologies — will deliver their quarterly results on Monday and Tuesday, respectively, after the bell. Both have tumbled sharply this month, with HPE down 25% and Dell off 34%, amid the sell-off among companies with exposure to the artificial intelligence buildout.
Meanwhile, electronics retailer Best Buy is set to deliver results before the bell on Tuesday, while software company Workday will share its financials after hours on the same day.
U.S. equity futures jumped to begin trading Sunday evening, seeking to rebound from Friday's sell-off.
Futures tied to the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 412 points, or 0.8%. S&P 500 futures advanced 1.1%, while Nasdaq-100 futures rose 1.9%.

Thanksgiving Gas Prices Could Break a Record Despite Recent Plunge
Fears of renewed U.S.-Iran hostilities…
Brent crude has broken back…
Analysts warn of higher oil…
Alex Kimani is a veteran finance writer, investor, engineer and researcher for Safehaven.com.
Oil prices have traded in a narrow range over the past few sessions as forecasts of a coming surplus collide with continued attacks and stalled diplomacy in the Middle East. A run of agency reports this month has pushed expectations toward oversupply and weighed on crude. Brent crude was up 1.1% at $92.88 per barrel at 11:50 a.m. ET on Thursday, well below its October levels above 110 dollars but little changed from the start of the week, while WTI crude gained 1.7% to 84.69 dollars per barrel. The International Energy Agency (IEA) said in its November Oil Market Report that the global oil market will return to surplus in the fourth quarter as Gulf exports recover faster than global demand. Global oil supply rose to 105.4 million barrels per day in October, and the agency now sees supply exceeding demand by 1.7 million bpd in Q4 2026, a swing from its previous forecast of a 1.8 million bpd deficit. The IEA raised its Q4 supply estimate by 3.3 million bpd from last month, cut its 2027 demand forecast by 80,000 bpd to 104.3 million bpd, and lowered the implied call on OPEC crude by 220,000 bpd to 20.8 million bpd.
The U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) has moved in the same direction . In October, it forecast a 700,000 bpd inventory draw in the fourth quarter. It now expects stocks to build in Q4 and to rise by an average of 3.5 million bpd in the first half of 2027, after drawing down for most of this year. The EIA estimates that crude production shut in across the Gulf fell to 2.5 million bpd in October, from 4.8 million bpd in September and a peak of 10.9 million bpd in May. OPEC said crude output from the OPEC+ alliance rose by roughly 2 million bpd in October, led by Saudi Arabia and Iraq.
Related: Thanksgiving Gas Prices Could Break a Record Despite Recent Plunge
Analysts at Standard Chartered caution that higher Gulf output does not yet mean more oil reaching buyers. Tanker shortages, damaged infrastructure and record freight rates are still holding back shipments, and inventories drained earlier this year have left little cushion. The bank also warns that the IEA’s surplus call is larger than any other agency’s, and that forecast surpluses in the past have often failed to arrive on schedule.
The agencies also disagree on demand. OPEC’s November report puts global oil demand at 108.3 million bpd in 2027, almost 4 million bpd above the IEA’s figure, and keeps its forecast for 2027 demand growth at 2.55 million bpd. The two agencies measure liquids differently, so the gap overstates the disagreement, but it remains wide. The IEA expects petrochemical feedstocks to drive most of next year’s growth, with little increase in gasoline and diesel use. The EIA expects global liquids demand to grow by 2 million bpd in 2027 after falling by about the same amount this year.
Standard Chartered says the demand question will decide how much of the returning Gulf supply the market can absorb. OPEC’s higher consumption forecast leaves room for far more barrels than the IEA’s. The bank expects continued attacks on shipping, maritime security risks and stalled talks to keep a geopolitical premium in prices and sustain volatility, but still sees crude prices falling through 2027 as the market slowly normalizes.
In natural gas, Standard Chartered expects European prices to hold at elevated levels through winter, even if milder weather on the continent and better LNG supply bring short-term relief. Europe has already drawn heavily on storage that started the season low: EU gas inventories stood at 70.4% on Nov. 15, about 18 percentage points below the five-year average. Qatar’s LNG exports roughly doubled in October from September but remain about two-thirds below their pre-war level, and QatarEnergy’s force majeure on European deliveries runs through December. Colder weather in Britain could also pull gas away from the continent, so Europe will still need steady imports to protect what is left in storage.
Dutch TTF front-month futures rose €2.25 to €83.10 per megawatt-hour on Thursday morning on an outage at Norway’s Troll gas field and cooler weather forecasts.

Editor's Note: This is a developing story.
An oil refinery in the city of Novoshakhtinsk, in Russia’s Rostov region, and an oil pumping station in Tatarstan were left burning after a large-scale attack by Ukrainian drones, multiple monitoring outlets reported early on Nov. 23.
The strikes are the latest Ukrainian attack on Russian energy sites aiming to reduce Moscow's oil profits and deplete fuel powering Russian forces.
Ukrainian open-source intelligence (OSINT) monitoring channels Exilenova+ and Supernova+ reported that the Novoshakhtinsk Oil Products Plant (NZNP) in Novoshakhtinsk, approximately 200 kilometers (125 miles) from Ukrainian-controlled territory, was struk in a Ukrainian drone attack.
Eyewitness footage from residents near the site appears to show fires from the facility glowing brightly in the night sky, with the sounds of Russian air defenses audible.
Yury Slyusar, Rostov Oblast's regional governor, confirmed that the region "was subjected to a massive aerial attack" overnight on Nov. 23.
Russian opposition news outlet Astra reported numerous explosions in the city and that residents of the region said the fire from the facility could be seen many kilometers away.
The Kyiv Independent can not independently verify the extent of the damage or the targets of the strikes at the time of publication.
The site has been the target of multiple Ukrainian attacks. On Sept. 25, the site was left in flames following a drone attack. On Aug. 25, the refinery was targeted in a strike , but no damage to the facility was immediately reported.
In October, an oil-loading terminal handling petroleum products for export, including shipments from the Novoshakhtinsk oil refinery, was left burning after a Ukrainian attack.
According to Ukraine's General Staff, the Novoshakhtinsk refinery can process approximately 7.5 million tons of oil per year. The plant is considered one of the important suppliers of petroleum products in southern Russia supplying the Russian armed forces.
1,533 km (953 miles) northweast of Novoshakhtinsk, Ukrainian forces also struck an oil pumping facility in Almetyevsk, Republic of Tatarstan. Exilenova+ reported that the Kaleykino Oil Pumping Station was targeted.
The facility is a key hub in Russia's oil transportation network, supplying crude oil to refineries and the Druzhba pipeline system. The station receives and blends crude oil from different Russian regions before distributing it to refineries and the Druzhba pipeline, which carries Russian oil to European markets.
Footage from the scene at Almetyevsk appeared to show flames illuminating the night sky.
Previously, Ukrainian forces struck three oil storage tanks at the Kaleykino facility on Nov. 19, with one storage tank catching fire and two others sustaining damage. Each tank has a capacity of 50,000 cubic meters of oil, making them among the largest storage facilities of their kind in Russia.
As Kyiv continues to pummel Russian energy sites, Moscow's oil output has seen a notable decline.
Since late October, Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refiners have decreased the country's crude oil processing volumes by 45% , Reuters reported on Nov. 18.
On Nov. 15, President Volodymyr Zelensky said that Ukrainian forces took 55% of Russia's oil refining capacity offline through long-distance drone and missile strikes.
Several people remain missing as rescue operations continue in Dymer, where a Russian drone destroyed part of a residential building on Nov. 22.
The plant is considered one of the important suppliers of petroleum products in southern Russia supplying the Russian armed forces.
In the newest announcement, the Lublin District Prosecutor’s Office revealed that debris from Kh-101 cruise missiles was discovered at three sites in eastern Poland: Nowy Lipowiec, Rudnik, and Mołodycz.
A petition for Kim's resignation has garnered 25,605 signatures, requiring the Cabinet of Ministers to review and respond within 10 days.
"The enemy is deliberately terrorizing the civilian population, attacking civilian infrastructure, and taking lives," Governor Tymur Tkachenko said.
Libyan officials have reported that the Russian Navy corvette Merkury was severely damaged by Ukrainian sea drones. Kyiv has not commented on the claim.
The drills focused on small drones, including first-person-view (FPV) models, Ukraine's General Staff said.
Repair crews are working to restore electricity, but continued Russian attacks and air raid alerts are disrupting their work, Ukraine's state-owned grid operator Ukrenergo said.
President Volodymyr Zelensky again urged Washington to authorize the transfer of Patriot missiles that Ukraine's allies have already paid for.
Ukraine's Air Force said Russian troops launched 186 attack drones against Ukraine overnight, of which 161 were shot down.
The number includes 2,310 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
Ahead of the reported attack, a temporary ground stop was imposed at Krasnodar Airport, officials reported, amid the presence of drones in the nearby airspace.
Kyiv and London finalized an agreement on Nov. 21 that will see the United Kingdom manufacture "middle strike" and long-range drones for Ukraine on British soil, Ukraine's Defense Ministry announced.

articles.title_orig: Molly Meldrum: Australian music legend dies aged 83
articles.title_zh: Molly Meldrum: Australian music legend dies aged 83
articles.content_orig:
Australian music industry legend Molly Meldrum has died aged 83 after a long illness.
The music promoter and broadcaster, born Ian Alexander Meldrum, helped define the nation's music tastes for decades, championing local artists like INXS and Kylie Minogue and global acts like Abba.
Known for his chaotic demeanour and trademark Stetson hat, he interviewed an array of stars from King Charles to Elton John, who described Meldrum as the "single most important influence in Australian pop music".
In a statement, Meldrum's family said he "passed away peacefully" at a hospital in Melbourne in the early hours of Monday morning.
"Affectionately dubbed 'the Guru', Molly was the heartbeat, the champion and the spirit of Australian music," the statement said.
Meldrum lived with an acquired brain injury after falling from a ladder in 2011.
Born in Victoria in 1943, he displayed a love of music from an early age and went on to host the Australian Broadcasting Corporation's music television programme Countdown, and later a segment on variety show Hey Hey, It's Saturday.
Meldrum in 2014 became the first person who was not a recording artist to be inducted into the Australian Recording Industry Association (Aria) Hall of Fame.
Among his most famous interviews was a 1977 sit-down with King Charles, in which Meldrum could not calm his jitters.
He stumbled over his lines, declaring: "Your Royal Highness... Oh, oh, I'm sweating like a pig".
King Charles reflected on the infamous interview for Countdown's 40th anniversary special , saying: "There is an old showbusiness saying which warns never to work with animals or children. But nobody prepared me for Molly Meldrum".
On Monday, Arts Minister Tony Burke said the country had lost an icon.
"One of his greatest legacies will be the generations of Australians who grew up with his unmistakable enthusiasm and love of music. A true champion of Australian talent, you will be missed, but never forgotten."

articles.title_orig: Automation system problem at Delta causes flight delays as Americans travel for Thanksgiving
articles.title_zh: Automation system problem at Delta causes flight delays as Americans travel for Thanksgiving
articles.content_orig:
Delta Air Lines has resolved an issue with its weight and balance system that caused nationwide delays leading into a busy Thanksgiving travel week, the airline said.
Calculating weight and balance on an aircraft is a critical part of the pre-departure preparations. Delta was forced to use “manual workarounds” on Sunday morning “to safely get flights departed,” the airline told CNN affiliate WSB-TV , as delays rippled across its network.
The system’s automation for departing flight weight and balance calculations is now working, Delta said. But passengers could still experience lingering effects from the holdup.
Over half of Delta’s total flights were delayed and 6% were canceled as of 9:30 p.m. ET on Sunday, according to flight tracking website FlightAware. Delta has said about 70% of Sunday’s schedule changes were due to the automation issue, which caused an hourslong ground delay at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport – Delta’s biggest travel hub and the busiest airport in the world .
The ground delay was canceled around 11:30 a.m. ET, according to an FAA advisory .
“Delta teams are focused on completing the remainder of today’s schedule. Cancellations, as always, are a last resort when all other options have been exhausted,” Delta told CNN, apologizing to customers for the delay in their travels.
Calculating weight and balance on an aircraft ensures the fully loaded aircraft is not too heavy to fly, is loaded properly and the pilots have the right settings for a safe takeoff.
Major airlines use sophisticated computer programs at their headquarters to calculate these numbers.
“Compliance with the weight and balance limits of any aircraft is critical to flight safety,” according to the FAA’s Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge .
For Delta, the weight and balance instructions for baggage crews are planned at the Operations and Customer Center in the Atlanta headquarters using a system called ALIS, or Automated Load Instruction System.
“Right now, it’s a system-wide outage for Delta Air Lines,” an employee explained to a pilot in Boston on Sunday morning in a radio call captured by ATC.com . “The ramp isn’t really able to load because there is no ramp worksheet in there, so that’s what we’re doing, we’re manually counting bags and doing a report for you guys.”
“Oh, geez,” the pilot responded.
“Kinda like the good old days across here,” the ramp worker noted sarcastically.
The Delta slowdowns come at the outset of what is projected to be a busy holiday travel period. Over four million travelers are expected at Delta’s Atlanta hub between November 19 and December 1, according to a news release from the airport.
Many travelers have already experienced long lines and frustrating disruptions in recent weeks after all flights nationwide were grounded just over a week ago, sparking flight delays and cancellations for several days.
The FAA has said the outages that triggered the nationwide ground stop likely stemmed from an outdated copper wire at a remote location.
Sunday’s Delta delays are not related to any FAA air traffic systems, the FAA confirmed in a social media post .
The ground delay affected Delta flights and was not airport-wide, a spokesperson for Hartsfield-Jackson told CNN in a statement.
More than 60% of flights out of Hartsfield-Jackson were delayed Sunday evening, according to FlightAware, while around half of inbound flights to the airport were also delayed. The data does not specify how many of these delays were Delta flights.
Atlanta resident Shane Rocha and her family were traveling through Hartsfield-Jackson on Sunday morning to visit family, Rocha told CNN affiliate WANF. Rocha said she had flown earlier in the week without any issues and was hoping that today’s travel would be equally smooth.
“Luckily we’re only 19 minutes delayed, knock on wood,” she said. “Hopefully it stays that low.”
Although the specifics surrounding the Delta issue remain unclear, United Airlines experienced an issue with its weight and balance computer system in 2025 that triggered more than 1,000 delays and dozens of cancellations, the airline said at the time.
United also experienced a brief system outage on November 16 that affected fewer than 150 flights across the US, the airline told CNN. This outage appears unrelated to Sunday’s Delta automation issue and the previous nationwide FAA ground stop.
At the time of United’s outage, the FAA said the incident was not an agency equipment issue and the airline said there is no indication it was cybersecurity-related.
Beyond system disruptions, severe weather in the Northeastern United States has caused headaches as many people travel for the upcoming Thanksgiving holiday.
Passengers flying to New York’s LaGuardia Airport and New Jersey’s Newark Liberty International Airport can expect around two hours of weather-related ground delays on average, according to FAA updates .
Weather has also sparked delays for flights to San Francisco, while San Diego and several Florida airports are experiencing departure hold-ups due to a high volume of flights.
This story has been updated with additional information.

articles.title_orig: China Finds Another Route to Protein -This Time From Industrial Gas
articles.title_zh: China Finds Another Route to Protein -This Time From Industrial Gas
articles.content_orig:
China's search for new ways to produce protein is taking another interesting turn. Researchers at the Tianjin Institute of Industrial Biotechnology are investigating how industrial gases can be converted into nutrients for microorganisms capable of producing protein. It's another indication China isn't betting on a single technology to strengthen its future food supply.
The process begins with syngas — a mixture of gases that can be generated from industrial processes or biomass. Through fermentation, microorganisms convert these gases into compounds including acetate, which can then feed a second fermentation process. Chinese researchers have been testing how this nutrient-rich liquid can support the growth of Yarrowia lipolytica , a yeast with potential applications in microbial protein production.
The early results are encouraging. Researchers reported a 7.7% improvement in yeast biomass production in a five-litre fermenter, alongside an increase in acetate conversion from 21.68% to 41.1%. These are laboratory-scale results, not evidence that commercially competitive food protein is about to reach supermarket shelves. Nevertheless, they demonstrate another possible route towards producing useful biomass without relying exclusively on conventional crops or livestock.
What makes this particularly interesting is the wider Chinese strategy. From precision fermentation and cultivated proteins to microbial biomass and alternative fermentation feedstocks, Chinese researchers are exploring multiple approaches to protein production. Each has different technical and economic challenges, but collectively they could expand the country's future production options.
For countries such as New Zealand, the question is worth asking: if protein can increasingly be produced using industrial carbon streams, microorganisms and controlled fermentation systems, how might that change the economics of food production and national food security? China appears determined to find out.
