articles.title_orig: San Francisco is enjoying an AI boom, but worries about a crash are growing
articles.title_zh: San Francisco is enjoying an AI boom, but worries about a crash are growing
articles.content_orig:
Lauren Goldboss is busy. The owner of a small San Francisco dog-walking company, she has been hiring staff and buying vans.
Fuelling the growth is her new office dog-walking service Paw Perk, popular with some local AI start-ups.
Her business is an example of how the AI boom in San Francisco is benefiting other sectors.
The city saw an exodus of residents during the pandemic and its downtown was weakened by remote work, but it s now enjoying a rejuvenation, with AI being the major driver.
Leading AI firms OpenAI and Anthropic – which have been hiring top engineering talent, often on eye-popping salaries – are based here. Anthropic, the company behind the Claude chatbot, last week listed on New York's Nasdaq stock exchange.
Thousands of other AI start-ups have also sprung up in San Francisco.
Signs of the boom are evident in soaring rents and house prices, falling office vacancies, and buses and billboards plastered with cryptic AI adverts.
But what if there is a significant downward correction in AI share prices and a resulting big fall in investment in the industry? The International Monetary Fund last month became the latest organization to warn that this was a possibility.
Concerns have since continued due to the scandal surrounding Jensen Huang, the former boss of AI firm Nvidia, based south of San Francisco, causing some wider AI stock falls. However, Nvidia remains highly profitable, and Wednesday of this week it reported that its latest quarterly profits had doubled from a year earlier to $65bn (£49bn).
What are the thoughts of AI workers in the city, and should San Francisco – no stranger to tech's boom-and-bust cycles – be preparing for a possible crash?
One AI worker, employed by one of the largest companies in the city, is convinced that a crash is coming. "I am certain that the house of cards will come down… and I'm sure it will affect me," says the man who asked that we didn't use his name.
He questions whether leading US AI companies can generate enough revenues to justify their enormous spending commitments as cheaper, increasingly capable AI models emerge, especially from China.
But he isn't losing sleep over it. "Why worry about things I can't control?"
Another San Francisco-based AI worker, who also asked to remain anonymous, says that a significant market correction is "totally possible".
Yet he adds that most people don't think of it as the core risk. Instead, he says that the bigger concern in his circles, and the one he shares, is the existential risk that AI could pose to humanity.
"In some weird way, a market correction being the worst-case outcome feels great."
If there is an AI crash, San Francisco could be hit far more than Silicon Valley which lies 40 miles to its south.
That's because the AI boom is very much centred on the city itself rather than the wider San Francisco Bay Area, which includes Silicon Valley.
One study found that 60% of all venture capital invested in US AI firms from 2023 to 2025 went to the companies located in San Francisco, dwarfing the significantly smaller percentage given to companies in Silicon Valley.
But some factors suggest that the impact of a crash in San Francisco may be softer than some fear.
For all the investment they have attracted, AI companies are employing relatively few workers in the city compared to previous tech booms. So there may not be that many jobs to lose in a downturn.
"Hiring isn't necessarily on the scale as we would have thought with the amount of venture capital and new company formation," says Jeff Bellisario, executive director of the Bay Area Council Economic Institute, a business-affiliated think tank.
Ted Egan, the chief economist for the City and County of San Francisco, adds that "because of AI, it is a good time for tech again in the city, but we are not seeing tonnes of overall tech job growth".
Despite the expansion of the AI sector, the city remains about 35,000 jobs shy of its pre-pandemic peak, estimates Enrico Moretti, an economics professor at the University of California, Berkeley.
Instead, much of the spending by AI firms in the US is going towards data centres and computing power, relatively little of which are located in the Bay Area. San Francisco might be the brains of the AI boom, but it isn't the brawn.
Nonetheless, a significant correction could still be "very painful" for San Francisco, warns Moretti. Less AI hiring and potential layoffs would ripple through the local service sector, likely to affect jobs in everything from restaurants, to retail, to personal services like dog walking.
"It is the spillover on service jobs that would actually be the main effect," he says.
Office vacancies could also rise, reducing downtown foot traffic, while rents and house prices could weaken.
But AI isn't the only force driving San Francisco's recovery. Healthcare and tourism – which the city has been working to encourage, including by improving downtown safety and cleanliness – are also growing, which may help cushion against a possible AI downturn.
"Tourism is not fully back, but the growth has been healthy," says Egan, adding that it is a sign of confidence in San Francisco.
All told, Egan doesn't expect an AI crash to fundamentally alter San Francisco's economic trajectory.
"The city's economy has not been screaming during this AI boom, so I wouldn't expect it to grind to a halt if there was a slowdown in AI spending," he says. "I think of it primarily as a hiccup that we should expect, rather than a major course correction for the city's economy."
As to whether and how San Francisco's city government should prepare, there are limits to what it can do, note Bellisario and Moretti. But encouraging growth in sectors beyond technology and maintaining financial reserves could help.
For Goldboss, the dog-walking company owner, her philosophy is to "build while it is here". If the next tech bust comes – "always a reality in San Francisco" – she will try to adapt to what the market needs. "It is just the risk you kind of have to take," she says.

articles.title_orig: Urgent warning issued to cruise passengers about strict new law in Mexico
articles.title_zh: Urgent warning issued to cruise passengers about strict new law in Mexico
articles.content_orig:
Clint Henderson, managing editor at The Points Guy, explains why cruise costs are climbing and why sailing can still offer vacationers good value.
Cruise passengers are being warned they may need to provide extensive documentation for onshore activities at ports in Mexico.
The sweeping law now requires adults traveling to Mexico with minors to prove their relationship to the children in the group, or face denial of service at hotels, resorts and tours, the "Royal Caribbean Blog" reported.
Effective Nov. 14, 2026, an amendment to Mexico's General Tourism Law places pressure on tourism providers to verify family relationships, according to Travel Market Report .
CRUISE TIPPING CHARGES ARE 'OUT OF CONTROL' SAY PASSENGERS AS COMPANIES TOUT 'EXCEPTIONAL SERVICE'
The Mexican Senate unanimously passed the measure to combat child trafficking and exploitation, aiming to shed the country's status as a major destination for such crimes.
"Pedophiles don't come to Mexico by chance," noted Sen. Laura Esquivel Torres, as reported by the same blog.
A change to Mexico's General Tourism Law places pressure on tourism providers to verify family relationships. Pictured here, Carnival cruise passengers disembark at Costa Maya Cruise Port in Mexico. (iStock)
"Starting today, we will begin to shut down these opportunities," Torres added.
Fox News Digital reached out to Sen. Torres and Royal Caribbean for additional information.
POPULAR CRUISE LINE'S BIKINI CRACKDOWN COULD SURPRISE PASSENGERS AT ISLAND PORTS
Tourism operators are legally required to check documents and must notify authorities if an adult cannot prove legal guardianship or parentage, according to news outlet TravelHost.
Travelers should be prepared to present passports, long-form birth certificates and custody or guardianship paperwork, the same blog noted.
When cruisers in Mexico, pictured here, disembark at a port, they are required to bring documentation proving minors are related to parents. (iStock)
Documentation explaining any differing last names between a parent and child is also recommended.
Even if cruise passengers are only stopping in a Mexican port for the day, the rules apply to all local services.
11-NIGHT CARIBBEAN CRUISE ABRUPTLY CANCELED AFTER COAST GUARD DETAINS SHIP
While simply disembarking from a cruise ship might not trigger a document check, booking a beach club day pass, a local snorkeling excursion or renting a vacation home likely will, the blog reported (it is not affiliated with Royal Caribbean).
When walking around shops in Costa Maya, Mexico, families must bring documentation explaining differing last names between a parent and child. (iStock)
Travelers are urged to call hotels and tour operators in advance to confirm paperwork requirements.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER
The Mexican government has not yet released an official checklist, but travel experts advise bringing a folder with these documents, according to the same blog:
Travelers have been taking to Reddit to weigh in on the new rules.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES
"This is going to be a mess," one person wrote.
"There has been no formal guidance given by the Mexican government on what will be accepted and different hotels (including different people at the same hotel) have been giving different answers," the same commenter added.
Royal Caribbean passengers disembarking from the Oasis of the Seas, pictured here, will require documentation for minors in Cozumel, Mexico. (iStock)
"Bring all government docs and letters from parent authorizing you to have [temporary] guardianship of their kids for travel," another Reddit user said. "Not that hard, really."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"I own a travel agency and [before that] was a Spanish teacher for 17 years. [I] traveled to Mexico with my students every summer and I always had a form for this — they used to often check," a third Reddit user said.
Cruise passengers on the Norwegian Joy cruise ship, pictured above, in Costa Maya, Mexico, will need documentation for minors. (Jeff Greenberg/Universal Images Group via Getty Images)
Another chimed in, "My only issue with using the birth [certificate] proof is that a passport and birth certificate are often the only, or certainly the two most important identity documents, a child has. Having both lost or stolen while out of the country would be very stressful to deal with."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"I also don’t understand why it matters for hotels," the Reddit user added.
Fox News Digital reached out to the Mexican Embassy in the United States, Mexico's Secretariat of Tourism and World Vision Mexico for more information.
Jessica Mekles is an editor on the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital.

articles.title_orig: Ukrainian city moves to remote learning as Russian strikes disrupt utilities
articles.title_zh: Ukrainian city moves to remote learning as Russian strikes disrupt utilities
articles.content_orig:
When American-led talks to end the war in Ukraine resumed last week in Abu Dhabi , the overriding question was whether Russia intended to give any ground after a nine-month lull in negotiations.
But Russian missiles and drones had already done the talking for Moscow, analysts said . Weeks earlier than expected, Russia has opened an intense bombing campaign against the infrastructure that keeps Ukrainians alive and functioning in the winter. Daily waves of strikes against Ukraine’s energy system have raised fears that the capital, Kyiv, a city of three million people, could become all but uninhabitable in the coming months.
In the Abu Dhabi talks, an emboldened Russia outlined hard-line demands that stood little chance of gaining acceptance by Ukraine and its European allies. That unbending stance indicated that Russia had no real interest in discussing peace now, because Moscow believes that the winter bombing campaign will strengthen its negotiating position entering the spring.
“They want to come to the table holding our energy system hostage,” President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine said after a recent Russian attack.
The Abu Dhabi talks will be followed by a meeting on Thursday between President Trump, President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia and the Chinese leader, Xi Jinping, at a summit in Shenzhen, China. It was unclear whether the three leaders would discuss the war in Ukraine.
Assaulting infrastructure has become Moscow’s strategy for victory as it has failed for nearly five years to achieve its major objectives in Ukraine. While Russia has tried each winter to knock out the country’s power system and freeze its people into submission, Ukrainian cities are now in their most precarious position of the war. The grid is more fragile after years of strikes, and the Ukrainian military is struggling to protect the system because of dwindling air defenses.

articles.title_orig: In September, she correctly said the stock market would fall; Now, the former Goldman Sachs analyst has another bold call
articles.title_zh: In September, she correctly said the stock market would fall; Now, the former Goldman Sachs analyst has another bold call
articles.content_orig:
The charts say that we’re just about short-term oversold and ready to bounce. Let’s take a look at the indicators to see when that bounce might happen and whether it will last.
You've reached your free article limit
You've read 0 of 1 free Pro articles.
Everyone sees it. How can they not see that we’re just about short-term oversold? When the S&P falls seven straight days, even folks who don’t even understand the concept (or pretend not to!) know the market is short-term oversold.
As you know, I have been eyeing that midweek (Tuesday/Wednesday) time frame for us to get short-term oversold. That has not changed. Many of the charts came right to the top of their spring gaps. I would love to see those gaps filled on Monday. Will we get it? I do not know.
For example, there is that gap on the chart of the SOX at 8000 (nice round number) that I am certain even my mother could see (and no, she has not called yet). There is also that gap on the chart of the QQQs at 590.
That doesn’t mean there isn’t some support in the areas the market closed on Friday, just that oftentimes gaps beckon to be filled.
But as you know, I prefer the indicators. The VIX is jumpy. Can it get jumpier? For sure. Friday’s put/call ratio chimed in at 1.13, which was also the third straight day of readings over 1.0, so we have finally got some put buying going on. The ten-day moving average of the put/call ratio is now .96, just shy of that July peak. I would not be surprised to see this climb higher in the coming days, but I can no longer scoff that it isn’t high enough. It goes on the positive side of the ledger now.
The QQQs chimed in with some serious volume at 134 million shares. This is the highest volume since the Taper Tantrum. It is also the second time we’ve seen over 100 million shares traded during this rout.
The Nasdaq McClellan Summation Index, which I use volume instead of breadth for, has been in a downtrend for months. As of Friday, it needs a net differential of +15 billion shares (up minus down volume) to stop going down. That is the highest since March of 2021. It’s extreme.
The DSI for both Nasdaq and the S&P are now at 9. Can they go lower? Yes, but my experience is that once this gets to single digits—and my indicators are oversold—we are due for a bounce.
What we don’t have is any positive divergences, as the number of stocks making new lows expanded to extreme levels on Friday, with Nasdaq the most extreme, at nearly 1300 stocks making new lows. Down below you will see the Nasdaq Hi-Lo Indicator is back into oversold territory.
I still think this is a bear market, and I suspect rebounds will get sold. I do not think we have extreme fear yet (there has still not been a day where everything gets sold and 90% of the volume is on the downside), but we are oversold, and we have enough of the short-term indicators that say expect a rally this week.
I will always turn toward the indexes if I am looking for an oversold rally. This time is no different. I’d go with the SMH (SOX) or QQQs. If you prefer not to play for a rally, then you can look to do some selling into the rally.
The Hi-Lo is discussed above.
Helene welcomes your questions about Top Stocks and her charting strategy and techniques. Please send an email directly to Helene with your questions. However, please remember that TheStreet.com Top Stocks is not intended to provide personalized investment advice. Email Helene here .
Down below, you will see I have been asked about a number of technology stocks. The only thing I see that can change their negative chart patterns would be if we see a huge gap up Monday morning that holds, and many of these charts leave Friday’s action as an island down below.
Xeris ( XERS ) is a light among darkness and hasn’t done a thing wrong except get overbought (in a panicky market, this would have been down last week). I’d say a correction is probably on the table if it trades under 16.
CRH ( CRH ) had a nice rally to resistance, and I would expect a bounce from that 83-85 area, but I think charts like this need to build bases, and that takes a long time. So an oversold bounce from that support is the best I see for now.
Agnico Eagle Mines ( AEM ) curiously has not made a lower low along with gold. And the DSI for gold is now 9. I would look for a bounce from this 145-150 area. Resistance is light at 160 and much heavier at 170’s gap fill.
Micron ( MU ) is oversold, and support is far away at 450. Resistance is at 650 and stronger at 700. Because I think the semis rally, I would love to see this down one more day before a rebound. If it cannot recapture 700, then I think on a longer-term basis this will head back to the 450 area.
My old friend Western Digital ( WDC ) finds itself with some decent support in the 250 area. If that breaks badly, then the next support (and measured target) is all the way down at 175.
Sandisk ( SNDK ) is into support near 70. Unless it can gap up over 95 and hold it (leaving Friday’s action as an island), then I’d look for resistance in that 95-100 area.
Netflix ( NFLX ) is perhaps indicative of this bear market. A former fan favorite that keeps enjoying terrific rallies but in the end just goes on to make lower lows. It’s oversold and at some support, but a rally into the low to mid 60s is about the best I think it can do at this moment in time.
Nebius ( NBIS ) is oversold, at support, and due for a bounce. I don’t even know where I would put resistance except in that 110-115 area. The question is if it can get that far.

articles.title_orig: China's industrial strength benefits global growth
articles.title_zh: China's industrial strength benefits global growth
articles.content_orig:
By MA SI in Shenzhen, Guangdong | 
          China Daily |
          Updated: 2026-11-23 07:26
China's manufacturing prowess is not "stealing jobs" from the rest of the world but creating shared opportunities through localized production, technology transfers and complementary trade, business leaders and experts said.
They made the comments during the 2026 APEC Economic Leaders' Week in Shenzhen, Guangdong province, pushing back against the so-called "China Shock 2.0" narrative that portrays the country's industrial rise as a zero-sum threat to global employment.
Wang Chuanfu, chairman and president of Chinese electric vehicle maker BYD, said many people outside China have some misconceptions about the country's manufacturing capabilities.
Citing BYD's operations in Chile, Wang said the company purchases large quantities of copper and lithium there and supplies Chinese electric buses that help improve the local environment.
"Our trade is complementary," he said. "We not only export Chinese technology to the world but also bring jobs and tax revenue to local communities, achieving mutually beneficial cooperation and win-win outcomes."
He said that the company's plant in Thailand, with an annual production capacity of 150,000 new energy vehicles, employs nearly 6,000 workers, more than 95 percent of them Thai. He added that most components are sourced locally. Similar arrangements exist at BYD's plants in Indonesia and Brazil.
"We work with 12,000 suppliers globally and aim to benefit the world with Chinese technology through local procurement and research and development," Wang said.
Lei Jun, CEO and chairman of Xiaomi, said, "Asia-Pacific economies form the world's core industrial and supply chain region and the most promising consumer market with strong complementarity and cooperation potential despite their differences."
The company's cars and smartphones require thousands of components, which can only be completed through global supply chain collaboration, he said. "Xiaomi cars will officially enter overseas markets next year," Lei added.
Noting that the automotive industry is a pillar industry in many countries, Lei said cooperating with local supply chains will enable products to better serve local consumers. "We will maintain an open mindset and deepen cooperation with local enterprises," he said.
The European market, including Germany, is among Xiaomi cars' overseas destinations in 2027, and the automaker has already signed memorandums of understanding with eight leading German automotive dealer groups.
Wang Zhisheng, vice-president of the China Chamber of Commerce to the EU, said: "Chinese companies are well aware of the importance of localization — moving from selling cars to Europe to building cars in Europe. We are creating abundant job opportunities for local communities."
BYD's Hungarian plant is set to begin mass production in the fourth quarter of 2026.
Liu Jincheng, founder and chairman of EVE Energy, a major Chinese lithium battery maker, said reaching consensus and co-construction are key aspects of Chinese companies going global.
EVE Energy has built a lithium battery plant in Malaysia and begun nickel resource operations in Indonesia, with nickel already in use in large quantities in luxury cars such as BMW. Its full-industry-chain project in Indonesia will bring electricity to more islands and villages, Liu said.
Li Jiaying, an associate research fellow at Renmin University of China's Chongyang Institute for Financial Studies, said China's real economy is not a source of crisis, but a pillar of global stability.
Describing the so-called "China Shock 2.0" as a deliberately crafted political narrative, Li said that it represents a self-preservation strategy adopted by certain countries confronting industrial disadvantages and domestic deindustrialization. Such countries employ public opinion smears and trade barriers to divert attention from their internal pressures.
Jostein Hauge, a political economist at the University of Cambridge, said the "China Shock 2.0" narrative is steeped in double standards and hegemonic anxiety, while intentionally understating the vast benefits that China's integration into the global economy has delivered to the world.

articles.title_orig: Israel’s new ground offensives test how little the world will do to protect Gaza
articles.title_zh: Israel’s new ground offensives test how little the world will do to protect Gaza
articles.content_orig:
Get unlimited access to Crikey. Now 70% off.
If you like this article, share it with your friends.
Israeli tanks and bulldozers crossed the Yellow Line in central Gaza last week, forcing Palestinian families to once again flee their homes.
Israel established this line in October 2025 to create a security buffer zone in Gaza, putting a pause on its war in the region. Agreed under the October 2025 ceasefire, the Yellow Line left Israel in control of 53% of Gaza. Israel has since pushed it west, and 2.1 million people are now concentrated within 128 square kilometres (an area smaller than Liechtenstein, which has a population of just over 40,000 people).
This provision was part of the agreement brokered by US President Donald Trump that facilitated the formation of the Board of Peace, a UN-endorsed body created to oversee the reconstruction and recovery of Gaza, with deliberate attention to Israel’s security concerns. This deal has been repeatedly violated: Hamas has not disarmed, and Israel has conducted multiple raids without making any public statements.
However, under the current caretaker leadership of Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel has made a deliberate point of announcing this most recent incursion to the world. This serves multiple purposes.
Domestically, Netanyahu needs to recover from Israel’s legislative election in October, which resulted in his rival Gadi Eisenkot from the centrist Yashar party being given the opportunity to form a coalition government . Eisenkot’s effort to do so could be significantly advanced by incorporating minor Arab-led parties in the Knesset.
By continuing, you agree to our Terms & Conditions and Privacy Policy .
That coalition would be difficult to negotiate in the shadow of another security flare-up in Gaza. Netanyahu sees national security as his trump card and has used it unsparingly to stoke public fear and anxiety. The Hamas attack on Israel in October 2023 was the best political lifeline for Netanyahu, and he leveraged it to keep public anxiety high and extend Israel’s military operations across the border to Iran, Lebanon and Syria.
The caretaker government has pitched the incursion squarely at its right-wing base. Defense Minister Israel Katz argued that Hamas continues to present a threat and that Israel will not withdraw until Hamas is dismantled. In his words , the Israel Defense Force is ready to take more land and make it “permanent parts of Israel’s security zones”.
This message resonates with the far right, which has been pushing for outright annexation of the Palestinian Occupied Territories, and reinforces ambitions for a Greater Israel that would swallow land belonging to neighbouring Arab states. Netanyahu is on the record as an advocate of that vision, putting the lie to any pretensions of allowing Palestinian sovereignty in the future. By keeping the security factor a live issue, Netanyahu hopes to make himself indispensable and gain advantage over his rival. Every security emergency gives his legal team grounds to pause his court trials.
Internationally, this is a brazen attempt to test Trump’s willingness to act on his plans.
The US president was a key advocate of the October 2025 ceasefire and the formation of the Board of Peace, which has been thwarted by Israeli non-cooperation ever since. Aid delivery to Gaza has remained a trickle as Israel cites security concerns. The plan promised at least 600 UN-coordinated aid trucks a day, but as of September 2026, the average was 49 , and only about 2% of convoys carried medical supplies. More than 150,000 tents and 500,000 blankets sit outside Gaza awaiting entry. More than 2,000 Palestinian patients have died waiting for medical transfer. This has led leading aid agencies to accuse Israel of pursuing “ displacement by design ”.
Board of Peace partners have pledged about US$18 billion to the reconstruction of Gaza. But Israel bars its technocratic administration from working in Gaza, and there is no indication this will change. This ongoing obstructionism and the refusal of Hamas to disarm were criticised in a Board of Peace report, issued before the latest incursion, that warned “a ceasefire that delivers nothing visible cannot be sustained indefinitely”. Trump is clearly frustrated but has not yet taken Netanyahu to task, as he is currently preoccupied with a crisis of his own making in the Persian Gulf. The latest Israeli incursion into Gaza may be a test of Trump’s willingness to act while Israel creates new facts on the ground.
This situation is a stain on the international community. No US official condemned the Israeli action, which coincided with a visit by the head of US Central Command, Admiral Brad Cooper, to Israel.
Israel has snubbed international rules of conduct and subjected a whole people to misery and death in full view of the world, without paying a price. The UN Security Council endorsed Trump’s plans for a ceasefire and the formation of the Board of Peace. Its silence now mocks its own vote. If Washington and the UN cannot enforce a deal they built, what credibility is left for the rules-based order?
Professor Dr Shahram Akbarzadeh FASSA is director of the Middle East Studies Forum at Deakin University, and author of Middle East Politics and International Relations: Crisis Zone — 2nd Ed .

articles.title_orig: Burnham to tell MPs 'landmark' EU deal could make next decade 'much better'
articles.title_zh: Burnham to tell MPs 'landmark' EU deal could make next decade 'much better'
articles.content_orig:
BRUSSELS — Britain and the European Union agreed Friday to remove barriers to trade and expand travel opportunities for young people as they pledged to rebuild their strained ties with an “ambitious and dynamic” relationship. But they left big decisions about softening or reversing Brexit for another day.
In a joint statement after a summit in Brussels, the U.K. and EU confirmed agreements that will scrap border checks on plant and animal products, cut carbon taxes on some exports by linking their emissions trading schemes and let 100,000 young adults from each side live and work in the other’s countries for up to three years.
Other areas remain a work in progress , with the two sides giving themselves six months to reach an agreement on the level of university fees for EU students in the U.K. and vice versa.
Friday’s summit was part of efforts to forge a closer relationship, a decade after Britain voted to leave the EU and six years after the divorce became final.
Supporters of Brexit argued that leaving the EU’s vast free-trade area and web of rules would let Britain take back control of its borders, laws and economy, and strike new trade deals around the world. Critics say Brexit has left Britain weaker and more isolated, and new deals with countries including Australia and Japan have not made up for the economic hit from erecting barriers between Britain and its closest and biggest economic partners.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the deal is “a turning point” in EU-U.K. relations, and U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham called it a “historic moment.”
“This is a good day for Britain, and this is a good day for Europe,” he said.
This was only the second EU-U.K. summit since Britain became the first country to leave the world’s biggest trading bloc. Months — likely years — of negotiations lie ahead on everything from electricity markets to manufacturing rules.
Burnham said the summit was a step toward undoing a decade of damage caused by the divorce.
He said the two sides are “rebuilding the bridges that were broken all of those years ago” and “building a much more constructive relationship with our nearest neighbors and our largest market.”
Burnham has said all options should be on the table for future relations, including rejoining the now 27-nation bloc. But he’s stressed that reversing Brexit is just one possible outcome , and far from imminent. It would need the backing not just of British voters, but the unanimous support of a mistrustful EU. Still, he has broken a long political code of silence on the option of rejoining.
“We remain open to have the closest possible relationship,” European Council President António Costa said. But he also recalled the obligations of EU membership, including single-market principles on the free movement of goods, services, people and capital.
Burnham pitched the package of agreements approved Friday as a way of “cutting costs, keeping prices down in the supermarkets and creating opportunities for young people .” He said the deals could bring in 17 billion pounds ($22 billion) a year and add 0.5% to Britain’s economic output.
British retailers welcomed the deal to remove checks on food and agricultural products, which will make it cheaper and easier for U.K. businesses to export to Europe.
“Getting our spaghetti bolognese from Lincolnshire onto a shelf in Dublin takes hundreds of extra miles, mountains of paperwork, a vet’s signature and even the Latin name of a cow,” said Alex Freudmann, managing director of food at Marks and Spencer.
Freudmann said Friday’s announcement “is a major step forward.”
But nothing in U.K.-EU relations is ever quick or simple. EU negotiators want European students to pay domestic fees if they study in Britain rather than the higher fees for foreign students, something the U.K. has resisted.
An EU official said negotiations had not been easy but they sensed good will to resolve the issue. The official was designated to brief reporters about the summit but only on condition that they not be named.
Talks are also continuing on Britain’s desire to be included in the bloc’s “made in Europe” rules, which favor European manufacturers for public projects over rivals from China or elsewhere.
To get the deals, the U.K. must accept some EU rules and standards that it has no role in setting. Supporters of Brexit say that undermines Britain’s independence.
Nigel Farage , leader of the euroskeptic, anti-immigration party Reform UK, told reporters in Brussels that Burnham had taken “the first step, incrementally, to take us back into membership of the European Union.”
The war in Ukraine, and the U.K.’s military strength, are drawing the two sides back together, and the summit produced pledges of stronger cooperation on security and defense, as well as efforts to restrict irregular migration.
Nevertheless, feelings remain raw , and EU officials have been reluctant to encourage talk of the U.K. rejoining. They are weary from the shifting demands of seven British prime ministers over the last decade and want clarity about the country’s intentions.
Von der Leyen said that a lot has changed in their relations since the Brexit vote, including the pandemic and Russia’s war on Ukraine. She said that the EU is “totally open to do the necessary brainstorming for the wider picture, the bigger picture” of what ties could look like in the future.
Burnham said he wanted the two sides to do that brainstorming before their next summit, probably a year from now.
For now, Burnham remains bound by the pledge made by Keir Starmer, his predecessor as Labour Party leader and prime minister, not to rejoin the bloc’s tariff-free customs union or frictionless single market, or to restore free movement for EU nationals to the U.K.
He acknowledged Friday’s agreements are “the limit of what we can achieve” before a national election.
“Incremental steps … only take us so far,” he said.

articles.title_orig: Equipment outage in Atlanta causes over 1,600 Delta flight delays - ABC News
articles.title_zh: Equipment outage in Atlanta causes over 1,600 Delta flight delays - ABC News
articles.source: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content_orig:
The delays were not the result of a systems hack, Delta said.
More than 1,600 Delta Air Lines flights nationwide were delayed on Sunday due to a technical issue causing an outage to one of the airline's weight and balance systems, according to Delta.
The equipment snafu comes as millions of people prepare to travel this week for the Thanksgiving holiday, and just days after the Federal Aviation Administration issued the second nationwide ground stop since the 9/11 terrorist attacks due to an equipment installation problem that caused telecommunications issues.
"These delays are not related to any FAA air traffic systems," the FAA said on Sunday about Delta's flight delays.
Delta said later Sunday afternoon that the weight and balance systems had returned to normal operation, and that the outage was not the result of a computer hack.
"Delta is rebooking customers to the next best itinerary and providing meals and hotel rooms where necessary," the airline said. "For customers facing a canceled flight and don’t wish to travel, refunds are being given."
Some 49% of all Delta flights Sunday were delayed by more than 15 minutes, Delta said, after the airline experienced an outage in a system used to calculate the weight and balance of departing flights, Delta said.
The majority of the delayed flights were at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport, but the equipment issue also affected flights to Atlanta from other airports, Delta said.
"Delta teams are using manual workarounds this morning to safely get flights departed while work continues to restore automation. We thank our customers for their patience and our people for their professionalism," Delta said in a statement earlier Sunday.

articles.title_orig: Tehran threatens to 'break legs' as 'Trump corridor' prepares to launch on Iran's border
articles.title_zh: Tehran threatens to 'break legs' as 'Trump corridor' prepares to launch on Iran's border
articles.content_orig:
Farzin Nadimi explains how the U.S. could target Iran’s remaining land routes — and why sealing them off will be a "mid- to long-term project."
Armenia is set to launch a U.S.-backed transportation and energy project along Iran's northern border Monday, despite warnings from a senior Iranian official that Tehran would "break their legs" if President Donald Trump and his allies crossed the Islamic Republic's "red line."
Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan confirmed that the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP) project would launch Monday, advancing the plan to connect mainland Azerbaijan with its Nakhchivan exclave through southern Armenia and establish energy links with Turkey and Azerbaijan, Turkish media reported, citing Interfax.
The project, a centerpiece of a U.S.-brokered peace initiative between Armenia and Azerbaijan, would also expand American economic involvement in the South Caucasus, where Iran has warned against any development it believes could threaten its security or regional influence.
TRUMP'S FIRST IRAN WAR ESCALATION POST-MIDTERM LOSSES SEEKS TO CHOKE OFF TEHRAN’S TRADE
US President Donald Trump (C), Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev (L) and Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan display the agreement they signed in the State Dining Room of the White House in Washington, DC on Aug. 8, 2025. US President Donald Trump said Friday that Armenia and Azerbaijan were committed to a permanent peace as he hosted a White House summit with the leaders of the two South Caucasus nations, which have fought for decades. (Photo by Andrew Caballero-Reynolds/AFP via Getty Images)
The corridor has also gained strategic significance amid the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran, as Tehran seeks to secure its northern trade routes and limit the U.S. security presence near its borders while Washington maintains its naval blockade and Task Force Iron Gate focuses on Iran's borders.
Speaking at the DigiTec 2026 technology conference in Yerevan, Pashinyan said the new TRIPP initiative, also known as the "Trump Corridor," would strengthen Armenia's regional energy connections, according to Interfax .
"Tomorrow we will officially announce the launch of the TRIPP program, and energy and electricity transit will be an important component of it," Pashinyan said during a public discussion on artificial intelligence.
"We will now connect our network to the electricity grids of Türkiye and Azerbaijan," he added.
The announcement followed a warning from Ali Akbar Velayati, a senior foreign policy adviser to Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, who accused Armenia of disregarding Tehran's security concerns over the proposed route.
"I told the Armenian ambassador the final word, clearly, that if Trump and his allies want to cross this Iranian red line, we will break their legs," Velayati wrote in a Nov. 5 article published by the Iranian newspaper Ettelaat, according to Iran's Tasnim News Agency .
TRUMP RETALIATES AFTER IRAN ATTACK AS EXPERT WARNS REGIME IS GROWING MORE DANGEROUS
A view from Armenia's southern border reveals the Arax River, with Iran visible across the water on May 2025. This crossing is a vital lifeline for Armenia, facilitating essential trade and energy flows, especially as tensions rise over the proposed Zangezur Corridor. Iran strongly opposes the corridor, fearing it would sever its direct land access to Armenia and diminish its role as a regional transit hub. The corridor, intended to connect Azerbaijan to its Nakhchivan exclave through Armenian territory, has become a flashpoint in regional geopolitics. (Anthony Pizzoferrato/Middle East Images/AFP via Getty Images)
Velayati also warned that Iran would defend its security interests in the South Caucasus regardless of Russia's involvement, pointing to Tehran's longstanding opposition to the proposed route.
The roughly 26-mile corridor would run through Armenia's southern Syunik province, near the Iranian border, connecting mainland Azerbaijan to Nakhchivan and providing an onward link to Turkey, a NATO member.
The route would include railways, roads, electricity transmission lines and fiber-optic cables, creating trade connections between Central Asia and Europe.
Iran has long opposed proposals for what Azerbaijan calls the "Zangezur Corridor," particularly arrangements that Tehran fears could weaken Armenia's control over the territory, disrupt Iran's access to Armenia or expand the presence of outside powers near its borders.
In August 2025, Velayati had already warned that the corridor could become a "graveyard" for what he called Trump's mercenaries, according to Al Jazeera .
"Such a corridor will turn into a graveyard of the mercenaries of Donald Trump, not a route owned by the U.S. president," Velayati said, according to the outlet.
Velayati also argued that Iran would act to protect the South Caucasus regardless of Moscow's position, while expressing his belief that Russia opposed the corridor on strategic grounds.
NO RETREAT AT HORMUZ — IRAN MUST NOT CONTROL THE WORLD’S ENERGY LIFELINE
Ali Akbar Velayati, a senior foreign policy adviser to Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, accused Armenia of disregarding Tehran's security concerns over the proposed route. (Photo by Rouzbeh Fouladi/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
During a December 2025 meeting with Armenia's ambassador to Tehran, Grigor Hakobyan, Velayati again raised concerns about the proposed route, according to Iran International .
The project emerged from a U.S.-brokered diplomatic initiative aimed at ending decades of conflict between Armenia and Azerbaijan over Nagorno-Karabakh, an internationally recognized part of Azerbaijan that was controlled for years by ethnic Armenian separatists before Azerbaijani forces retook the territory in 2023.
Trump had hosted Pashinyan and Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev at the White House in 2025, where the two leaders signed a joint declaration intended to advance peace, normalize relations and reopen regional transportation links.
The declaration established the basis for the TRIPP initiative, giving Washington a central role in developing infrastructure.
Under the implementation framework announced by Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Armenian Foreign Minister Ararat Mirzoyan in January, the TRIPP Development Company would oversee development of the infrastructure.
TRUMP MEETS KEY IRAN WAR MEDIATOR AS UAE REVEALS MAJOR OIL EXPORT SURGE DESPITE CONFLICT
Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan confirmed that the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP) project would officially launch Nov. 23. (Photo by ANDREW CABALLERO-REYNOLDS/AFP via Getty Images)
The framework calls for a U.S.-controlled entity to hold a 74% ownership stake in the company, with Armenia retaining 26%.
The company would receive development rights for an initial 49-year period , with an option for a further 50-year extension. Under the proposed extension, Armenia's ownership stake would increase to 49%.
Armenian authorities would retain jurisdiction over the territory, including responsibility for customs, immigration, law enforcement and border security.
The framework also provides for private operators to help facilitate trade and transit, while final customs and security decisions would remain with Armenian authorities.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
On Oct. 28, Armenia's parliament ratified the agreement by a vote of 63-32. Armenian President Vahagn Khachaturyan signed the ratification law Nov. 12.
The United States, Armenia and Azerbaijan also announced the launch of trilateral technical planning groups in November to advance the initiative.
Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

articles.title_orig: US targets AI chip exports to China, impacting Southeast Asia cloud firms
articles.title_zh: US targets AI chip exports to China, impacting Southeast Asia cloud firms
articles.content_orig:
Trump says he won't allow American companies to build data centres "outside" the US
Donald Trump has said he will ban US companies from building AI data centres overseas, threatening a "tremendous tax" for tech firms who do so.
"We're going to keep it all in this country," the US president said, while providing little detail on the potential policy he said others in his cabinet were hearing about for the first time.
Data centres were a central issue in the midterm elections earlier in November, with many Democratic candidates promising tougher regulation on their construction.
Tech giants including Meta and Google have entered agreements to build data centres overseas. It remains unclear how such a policy would be enforced if it was brought in.
"We're not going to allow our companies to build data centres outside of our country," Trump told reporters in a press briefing following his return from his trip to Asia.
"Because China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen."
But whether that idea will become policy remains unclear.
"I don't know if that's a breaking story, but I haven't even said that to my people. But I'm telling them now, they're here," he said.
Trump floated the policy after saying the US was leading on data centre construction, and he would not allow China to beat the US when it came to AI - which he calls super intelligence, or SI.
It also follows an announcement earlier this week that would restrict the export of advanced computer chips and who can access the computing power provided by them.
Washington on Monday announced firms would require a licence to buy advanced chips, so US officials can monitor whether they are being used to serve Chinese companies or they are being smuggled into China.
The move will impact South East Asian countries that have invested heavily in data centres, as Chinese companies seek to rent computing power from overseas.
Why Canada is embracing AI data centres while the US pushes back
Data centres are crucial to the AI boom. The vast warehouse-style buildings house the advanced computer chips and servers that are needed to run AI programmes such as Claude and ChatGPT.
As of April there were about 3,000 data centres across the US, with another 1,500 in various stages of approval and construction, according to the Pew Research Centre.
Many of them are built in rural areas, and concerns about issues including noise pollution and energy consumption helped drive Democratic candidates promising tougher rules on data centre construction to wins on 3 November.
"You ought to take advantage of the data centres. Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but take advantage don't shut them off," Trump said.
"We have a lot of places that want them badly, and they're great places. They have energy and they have everything. They're tremendous assets."
Large tech firms - often called AI hyperscalers due to the size of their investments in AI - have also been branching out, and Canada has made moves to step in to offer itself as an alternative location for these sites, with less local pushback against projects so far.
Meta has already broken ground on a data centre , external in the province of Alberta, and Anthropic has signed a long-term agreement to lease a proposed data centre in Nova Scotia.
The BBC has reached out to Meta for comment on Trump's remarks.
In September Google announced a â¬13bn ($15bn: Â£11bn) investment in AI infrastructure in Finland, which included funding for three data centres.
Last month, building work for two of those centres was halted due to concerns over the clearance of more than 300 hectares of forest.
Trump called out the build in Finland specifically, saying his administration was "not allowing that to happen".
Google has been contacted for comment.

articles.title_orig: U.S. trade chief sees progress in Canada talks, raises China concerns
articles.title_zh: U.S. trade chief sees progress in Canada talks, raises China concerns
articles.content_orig:
Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney shakes hands with China's President Xi Jinping at the APEC summit on Nov. 19, 2026.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is placing particular focus on renewing relations with China as he aims to deepen international trade ties and diversify from U.S. reliance amid a three-month-long trade war with the U.S.
When asked what cards Canada holds in its ongoing talks with Washington, Carney, who recently announced a new partnership with the E.U. , pointed to the country's budding relationships elsewhere.
“Our cards are that everyone else in the world wants to deal with us,” he said Wednesday during a remote interview with the New York Times from Shenzhen, China, where he was among the world leaders attending the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit . "If the U.S. doesn't want to do the deal, we're busy.” His remarks came in the wake of President Donald Trump's claim that the U.S. holds “all the cards” after trade talks collapsed in August, leading to both sides enforcing heavy retaliatory tariffs .
Carney and Trump had a meeting on the sidelines of APEC, but aside from a commitment to “continue” negotiations and stay in close contact, no progress was made. However, Carney painted his meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping in a much more positive light. Ahead of the summit, Carney and Xi announced a Canada-China trade pact , which provided additional tariff relief on Canadian food and agricultural exports into China, and in return saw Canada agree to extend tariff exemptions for certain Chinese steel and aluminum products by two years.
Carney, who is promoting a “Canada Strong” platform as he aims to build economic resilience at home, touted the expansion of the trade arrangement with China as something that will deliver “greater certainty and prosperity for all Canadians.” He also praised the negotiation process with China, saying: “They’re very professional. They move forward in a very linear fashion.”
In an eight-day tour that took him from a European summit in Ireland to the Philippines, Cambodia, and finally China for the APEC gathering, Carney forged ahead with his plan to diversify Canada's economy away from its dependence on the U.S., which by far remains the country's largest trading partner .
Experts say Canada's progress in deepening its economic relationships with China could challenge Trump's insistence that Washington holds the upper hand in trade negotiations.
“Part of the Trump Administration’s [belief] is that everybody needs the U.S. more than anything else, and therefore the U.S. has maximum leverage,” says Jennifer Hillman, co-director of the Institute of International Economic Law at Georgetown University. “What this is clearly saying is that Canada can afford to be less willing to give the U.S. whatever it asks for [in negotiations], because they have other options.”
China has the world's second-largest economy , behind only the U.S., giving it the potential to become a much larger market for Canadian goods than some of the other countries Carney has sought to deepen relations with.
“China represents a very big market and the potential of a really big trading partner,” says Lori Turnbull, a professor in the Faculty of Management at Dalhousie University, noting it could be a leverage point in U.S. negotiations. “Doing a deal with a country like China is something that [the U.S.] will care about because of the size of China's economy and its competitive relationship with the U.S.”
Carney's latest push to strengthen trade ties with Beijing forms part of a months-long effort to renew Canada-China relations. In January, he met with Xi to forge what he called a “ new strategic partnership ,” agreeing to allow in up to 49,000 Chinese electric vehicles at a tariff of 6.1%, rather than the previous 100% levy. China agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural products, including canola seeds, a major Canadian export.
The move drew criticism from Trump, who said that “China will eat Canada alive, completely devour it, including the destruction of their businesses, social fabric, and general way of life.”
While Canada's closer relationship with China could strengthen its hand in negotiations, experts also warn that it could backfire.
Turnbull points to the latest agreement to extend tariff exemptions on Chinese steel and aluminum as a potential source of tension with Washington. “Things like reducing tariffs on select steel and aluminum products coming from China is something that might make the U.S. and not just Donald Trump, but also [U.S. Trade Representative] Jamieson Greer angry,” she suggests.
Steel, aluminum, and auto tariffs were among the major points of contention when U.S.-Canada trade negotiations broke down in August, with both sides accusing each other of walking back commitments.
Carney, however, has played down concerns that Canada's growing trade relationship with China is a major issue for Trump.
“In my conversation with the President, he’s tried to understand where we are with China, where we’re going with China,” said Carney during a news conference in Shenzhen. “I shouldn’t speak for him, but in his hierarchy of issues, it’s not the top issue at all.”
Meanwhile, some Canadian officials have voiced concerns on expanding trade with China.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford warned Carney on Monday against opening the door for more Chinese-made EV vehicles in Canada, arguing the “government’s focus needs to be on protecting Canadian auto workers, not undermining them by importing even more state-subsidized cheap Chinese cars.”
Michael Chong, a lawmaker from Canada’s Conservative Party, during a press conference on Wednesday supported maintaining a dialogue with Beijing, but described Carney’s budding strategic partnership with China as a “risky gambit,” citing potential “national security” concerns.
In 2025, Ottawa identified China as one of the main perpetrators of foreign interference and espionage against Canada alongside other countries such as Russia and Iran. The Canadian government’s own analysis of Canada-China relations also points out that there are "associated risks” in broader trade cooperation in key areas, such as “prevalent and persistent intellectual property theft, and the risk of diversion of sensitive goods and technologies intended for civilian use for military purposes and applications.”
Carney said ahead of his Asia trip that he would raise concerns about foreign interference in his meeting with Xi. "The advantage of these meetings is you can raise issues directly and frankly,” he told reporters in Montreal on Nov. 10. Carney added that he would stress the importance Canada places on "the non-interference in our affairs by China and other countries.”
In a press briefing during the APEC summit, Carney emphasized that Canada's trade with China is largely focused on commodities, rather than sensitive technologies such as advanced semiconductors.
“We are exporting canola, we are exporting pork. We are exporting halibut,” Carney said , also citing liquefied natural gas and oil. “These are important industries. These are not cutting-edge semi-conductors.”
Experts point out that Canada could pursue deeper cooperation with other international partners in sectors where a closer relationship with China would be more difficult, including defense and advanced technology.
“[Canada] is not going to partner with China on defense, security, AI, and digital technology, things like that would be very difficult. [Carney] would have an impossible time trying to convince Canadians that's what we should be doing,” says Turnbull. “For those things, [Canada] would be putting [its] arms around the European Union.”
In September, the European Union unveiled its vision for Canada to become an “associate member” of the bloc. During an E.U.-Canada summit in Montreal in October, the two sides underscored their commitment to this plan, paving the way for deeper cooperation in areas including A

articles.title_orig: Netanyahu’s Likud, Eisenkot’s Yashar end coalition talks without deal
articles.title_zh: Netanyahu’s Likud, Eisenkot’s Yashar end coalition talks without deal
articles.content_orig:
Talks between the parties of caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot to form a unity government have ended without a deal.
Representatives of Netanyahu’s Likud and Eisenkot’s Yashar parties met in a Herzliya hotel on Sunday, where they remained split on who would lead the next government and whether far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir would be part of it, according to Israel’s Channel 12 broadcaster.
The Yedioth Ahronoth newspaper reported that Likud wanted Ben-Gvir in government, while Yashar insisted on his exclusion.
In a joint statement, the two parties said they had “outlined their positions on a range of substantive issues” and that a “follow-up meeting would be held”, without revealing a date or any further details.
Eisenkot has until December 6 to form a government, with the possibility of a 14-day extension, after the elections in October gave his bloc 48 seats – 13 short of a majority.
Netanyahu has called for a unity government , saying it was the only way that Israel’s security could be guaranteed. Such an arrangement would allow a government to be formed without the inclusion of parties led by Palestinian citizens of Israel, which won a record 19 seats.
Channel 12 reported that former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett, who leads the Together list, proposed a coalition of Together, Yashar, Likud and Avigdor Lieberman’s Yisrael Beiteinu, with Eisenkot serving first and Netanyahu succeeding him.
However, Eisenkot has opposed a rotation, and Netanyahu has reportedly insisted on taking the premiership first, while Lieberman has ruled out joining any government that includes Netanyahu altogether.
If unity talks fail, Yashar plans to seek a confidence vote in the Knesset for a minority government before Eisenkot’s mandate expires. It would rely on outside support from the Arab Joint List, led by Yousef Jabareen, and the United Arab List, led by Mansour Abbas.

articles.title_orig: Trump administration approved shipment of nearly 900,000 AI chips to China
articles.title_zh: Trump administration approved shipment of nearly 900,000 AI chips to China
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump on Friday said he and Chinese leader Xi Jinping discussed their shared affinity for former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang during their talks in China this week. Earlier in the day, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the ousted leader was not mentioned in separate talks he had with Chinese officials.
"I did discuss that with President Xi, and he said, 'Oh, brilliant, brilliant! He's a brilliant man.' He is," Trump said at a White House press conference.
Asked earlier Friday on CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" if Huang, a close ally of Trump 's, had come up in "any of your discussions with the Chinese," Bessent said "no," without elaborating.
A senior Trump administration official later said that both Trump's and Bessent's remarks were correct, and that both were addressing their own conversations. The official spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss those conversations.
Trump also reiterated that he would like to see Huang — who was replaced by interim CEO Colette Kress after resigning amid allegations of an extramarital affair with a Chinese spy — be restored as Nvidia's CEO.
"I would love to see Jensen be given a second chance," Trump said. "You know, we're a country of second chances, and I'd love to be able to see him. That's a very important company to us, and he put us in a position where we are literally 10 years advanced over other companies."
Nvidia's board is not considering bringing Huang back , a person familiar with the matter told CNBC earlier this week.
The president's comments came amid growing scrutiny of advanced U.S. chips, including those made by Nvidia, ending up in China either legally or by being diverted via third countries.
Both Trump's and Bessent's remarks are potentially an indication that the Trump administration may not focus on cracking down on China's efforts to acquire advanced chips.
Bessent suggested that U.S. policy allowing the sale of Nvidia's powerful H200 AI chips to China remains unchanged following the talks in Shenzhen this week.
"We've already agreed that the ... H200s are the threshold level of chips that could be sold to the Chinese, and, you know, that continues as planned," Bessent said.
"I wouldn't anticipate any change in the policy," he added after CNBC's Sara Eisen noted that Nvidia said it had stopped selling H200s to China.
The administration ignoring the subject of Huang's affair with a possible Chinese spy — whose Singapore-based company Megaspeed has been accused of acting as a cutout for Beijing — contrasts with the importance Trump has placed on beating China in the race to artificial intelligence dominance. It could suggest that despite his support for the U.S. AI industry, Trump is less concerned with addressing China's ongoing efforts to acquire U.S. semiconductors.
Trump has also defended Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick , who has come under fire from multiple directions for reportedly slow-walking export restrictions on Chinese chip sales. "I understand both sides of it," Trump said on Monday when he also said he's like to see Huang back as CEO.
Bessent's appearance on CNBC came after Trump's return from a tour through Asia that saw him meet with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China.
The meeting was historic as the first time the leaders of the three countries had met without other nations' counterparts. But the trilateral summit appeared to yield few deliverables on any number of the most pressing global issues related to the countries, including the Ukraine and Iran wars or the ongoing AI race.
Bessent told CNBC on Friday that there was a "robust discussion" between Trump and Xi on trade policy and AI.
They "agreed that humans should always be involved in any military decisions that SI makes, and the SI should not be allowed to be autonomous for major military actions," he said, abbreviating the term "super intelligence," Trump's attempted rebrand of AI.
In a CNBC appearance last week, Bessent lamented the "leakage" of U.S.-made AI chips to China and blamed the Commerce Department , led by Lutnick, for slow-walking export controls on suspected Chinese cutouts like Megaspeed.
Multiple Trump administration leaders have long sought to impose export restrictions on Megaspeed, but Commerce "has the pen" and "you will have to ask them about their internal processes," Bessent said in that interview.
On Friday, however, Bessent was much more tight-lipped.
Asked if there is a dispute between him and Lutnick over how aggressively the U.S. should be pursuing Chinese export controls, Bessent said, "I think we're all committed to following President Trump's instructions."
"I think we are going to see that the ... proper chip restrictions are in place, and the remote access has been curtailed," he added. Commerce recently took steps to close one of China's paths to accessing AI processors.
Correction: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent spoke to CNBC's "Squawk on the Street." A previous version of this story misstated the name of the show.
Editor's note: This story and headline have been updated following additional information provided by the Trump administration about the nature of Bessent's and Trump's meetings in China.

articles.content_orig:

Dictators around the globe, some of whom President Donald Trump says heâs âfallen in loveâ with, are growing fed up with the president over his chaotic leadership, a historian revealed.
Speaking on The Daily Beast Podcast , author Simon Sebag Montefiore said that Trumpâs relationships with various autocrats are less about genuine personal affection and more about his awe for their immense power over their countries.
He noted that while Trump has still shown affection for autocratic leaders like Russiaâs Vladimir Putin, Chinaâs Xi Jinping, and leaders in Arab countries, it hasnât been completely reciprocated back in his second term.
Photo Illustration by Victoria Sunday/The Daily Beast/Getty Images
âObviously they have some sort of affinity and, we donât know the details of what it is. I suspect itâs less, letâs say, romantic and exciting than many people like to think. By which I mean, I donât think itâs a meeting of the minds. I donât think it has much warmth or passion âat least from Putinâs side,â Montefiore explained.
âI suspect that when the Russians look at Donald Trump, and Iâm sure this is also true of the Chinese, and I know this is true in the Arab worldâ¦ but I think all of them, youâd have thought that theyâd all be thrilled by the election of Trump, and in some ways they are. But the one thing all these people hate really is spreading disorder, because that can also encompass them and overwhelm them,â he continued.
The White House did not immediately respond to the Daily Beastâs request for comment.
Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and U.S. President Donald Trump held a trilateral meeting in China last week.
Montefiore explained to host Joanna Coles that many of these leaders, namely Xi and Putin, are very weary of the disorder and chaos that they have experienced growing up and as young men, so they are uneased by the chaotic leadership style that Trump displays.
âIf I was to put on my hat as an amateur psychologist, I would say that, you know, Trump grew up, you know, admiring powerful people, worshiping powerful people and aspiring to that power,â he explained, adding âhe talked the language of mafia bosses, but, you know, the real mafia bosses are the leaders of autocracies where they really can order people to be whacked when they want.
âSo in some ways, you know, Trumpâs attraction to people like Kim Jong-un and Xi and Putin is that sort of almost boyish admiration for raw power,â he continued.
He added a counterpoint, saying that âon the other hand also, think that they, know, Putin and people like Xi and Putin, and again, the monarchs in the Arab world and dictators in the Arab world are quite alarmed by Putin, quite alarmed by Trump, and they hate unpredictability and they hate erratic decision-making.â
Autocrats like Saudi Crown Prince and Prime Minister Mohammed bin Salman don't like Trump's erratic leadership style.
Jessica Koscielniak/REUTERS
âSo, initially when he came to power, the view in the Arab world was, surprisingly, this man is wild, is extremely pro-Israel,â he continued.
But he said the Arab world realized that this âcould suit us because weâre exhausted with the hypocrisy of American, traditional American leaders who are equally, in some ways, hard to handle.
âAfter all, they say one thing and do another, and this might be easier for us to do business with,â he elaborated.
He went on, âAnd it looked like that in Trump one. In Trump two, I think theyâve walked back that to find Trump a worry and an alarm. And I know that their general attitude is like, they just wanna get through this intact somehow with all the erratic twists and turns.â

articles.title_orig: I stopped talking to my husband and let AI do it instead. He didn’t even notice | Polly Hudson
articles.title_zh: I stopped talking to my husband and let AI do it instead. He didn’t even notice | Polly Hudson
articles.content_orig:
iOS 27 gives the Messages app a variety of welcome upgrades , including one I’ve found myself using a lot: a Smart Reply feature that’s now personalized to the user’s writing style.
When the first wave of Apple Intelligence features were announced in 2024, one that I immediately thought sounded useful was Smart Reply.
The idea behind Smart Reply is simple. Rather than needing to manually type out replies in Messages and Mail, your iPhone can offer prewritten replies you can choose and send with a couple taps.
Great in theory, but the ‘Smart’ part of Smart Reply struggled to materialize in iOS 18.
Fortunately, with a key Apple Intelligence upgrade in iOS 27, the new version of the feature finally lives up to its name. Per Apple :
Smart Reply in Mail and Messages can now draw on a user’s personalized writing style.
Before, Smart Reply would look at the context of a conversation to craft its suggestions. But now, it also aims to match your writing style, punctuation, and tone.
In iOS 18, I almost never used Smart Reply. That’s because despite being fine at suggesting replies that technically worked, those suggestions didn’t sound like me at all.
That’s changed in iOS 27. Smart Reply now consistently impresses me. It no longer offers generic responses that sound like AI wrote them. Instead, its suggestions actually fit with my normal style of communication.
The only drawback is that right now, you’ll only ever see two Smart Reply suggestions. If Apple expanded the feature by letting you scroll horizontally through more options, I suspect I’d use Smart Reply even more.
Have you been using iOS 27’s Smart Reply feature in Messages? Let us know in the comments.

articles.title_orig: Ferrari's New 296 Challenge Stradale Is A 670-HP Race Car You Can Drive Home
articles.title_zh: Ferrari's New 296 Challenge Stradale Is A 670-HP Race Car You Can Drive Home
articles.content_orig:
The curtains open, and for a moment, you're completely transfixed. You know right away that you're looking at something special. This car represents a turning point for Ferrari, a significant departure from what came before. It's a genuine race car that's still somehow legal to drive on the street.
"This is a disruption of balance," says one of the people most closely involved in bringing the car to life. It's easy to see what he means. Even standing still, the Ferrari 296 Challenge Stradale looks like a car built with one thing in mind: setting lap times.
Ferrari even calls it "the production car with the closest connection to a competition vehicle."
No hybrid system. 670 horsepower. Just 2,932 pounds. And 1,360 pounds of downforce at 155 miles per hour. The car was developed alongside the 296 Challenge Evo , which will compete in Ferrari's one-make racing series starting in 2027. The price? Around $307,000.
Ferrari 296 Challenge Stradale
"It's a physical car, fundamentally different to drive. It's not like the 296 Speciale , which is easier and more immediate." Those two sentences tell you almost everything you need to know.
The Speciale is incredibly fast, but it's also approachable. Its electric motor helps with corner exits, drifting, and straight-line acceleration. The Challenge Stradale does away with all of that. There's no hybrid system and no electric motor to fill in the gaps. It's a raw, uncompromising machine with a narrower margin for error, one that relies on aerodynamics to do much of the heavy lifting.
The connection between Ferrari's road cars and its racing program goes back to the company's roots. Enzo Ferrari lived for competition, and in the early days, building road cars was largely a way to fund his racing ambitions. That relationship continues today through the Ferrari Challenge, a customer racing series that has been running since 1993.
It started with the 348, followed by the F355, 360, and every generation since. The 296 Challenge Stradale brings that racing DNA closer to the road than any production Ferrari before it.
Under the hood is the familiar twin-turbocharged 3.0-liter V6 from the 296, with both turbochargers mounted inside the V. The difference is that it now works entirely on its own, producing:
For comparison, the competition-focused 296 Challenge Evo produces 700 hp.
The turbochargers are carried over from the 296 Challenge, as are the thermal barriers. Ferrari focused its development work on boost pressure, variable valve timing, and insulation. The result is a dynamic torque increase of more than 32 percent compared to the 296 GTB. Without an electric motor smoothing things out, throttle response is also much sharper.
The eight-speed dual-clutch transmission has two distinct personalities. Push the car hard, and it switches to the aggressive shifting logic from the 296 Challenge, delivering gear changes in around 170 milliseconds. At lower speeds, it adopts a smoother calibration borrowed from the SF90 XX Stradale. The exhaust note builds all the way to 8,500 rpm, exiting through twin tailpipes derived from the race car.
Performance is predictably serious. The 296 Challenge Stradale hits 60 mph in 2.8 seconds, reaches 124 mph in 7.9 seconds, and tops out at more than 186 mph. Around Ferrari's Fiorano test track, it completes a lap in 1 minute and 18.5 seconds.
The dry weight is just 2,932 pounds with optional equipment, making it 308 pounds lighter than the 296 GTB. That's also the same figure as the 296 Challenge Evo. The result is a power-to-weight ratio of 4.37 pounds per horsepower.
A big part of the weight savings comes from removing the battery and electric motor. Ferrari also fitted a dedicated transmission with a lighter shaft and casing. Then there's the carbon fiber, which appears throughout the car:
For the first time on a production Ferrari, buyers can also request removable seat coverings, leaving parts of the underlying structure exposed.
One figure says a lot about how the Challenge Stradale behaves through corners: body roll is down 68 percent compared to the 296 GTB. Lateral performance improves by 7 percent, while stability increases by 34 percent.
The springs are roughly twice as stiff, requiring an additional spring mounted in series with the main one. It's a setup borrowed directly from the 296 Challenge Evo. The semi-active dampers also get two additional rebound settings, allowing Ferrari to retain at least some compliance when driving on public roads.
The car rides on Pirelli P Zero R tires, with semi-slick P Zero Trofeo RS tires available as an option. Both were specifically developed for the car.
With no regenerative braking system to rely on, stopping power comes entirely from the carbon-ceramic brakes. The front discs measure 15.7 x 1.5 inches, while the rear ones measure 15 x 1.3 inches. Ferrari says the car can stop from 124 mph in just 331 feet.
The traction control system is predictive and calibrated specifically for track driving, marking a first for a road-going Ferrari. It's all managed by the FIVE system, derived from the one used in the F80.
The headline aerodynamic figure is 1,360 pounds of downforce at 155 mph, a 72 percent increase over the 296 GTB. Ferrari achieves this through several carefully designed elements:
At the rear, a fixed wing derived from the 296 Challenge Evo generates 595 pounds of downforce on its own. There's one notable difference, though. Unlike the race car, the wing doesn't use a swan-neck mounting design. Instead, its supports attach from underneath to meet road homologation requirements, particularly those in the United States.
Ferrari's Centro Stile, led by Flavio Manzoni, took the clean design of the 296 and gave it a much more aggressive makeover. A technical insert on the hood, a wing suspended between two bumper-mounted "claws" inspired by the Evo, black metal mesh at the rear, and a double-keel diffuser all serve the same purpose. Here, form follows function.
Buyers looking to make their cars stand out can choose from a dedicated livery, three matte-finish wheel options, and even colored tire inserts through Pirelli's Color Edition program.
The Ferrari 296 Challenge Stradale starts at approximately $307,000.
